text: The force on the piston passes through the connecting rod to the crank on the crankshaft, producing a turning effect.
Torque measures the turning effect of force: it is calculated using the force and its effective lever arm, the perpendicular distance from the axis to the line of action.
Brakes produce torque opposing rotation; engine driving torque instead comes from the force on the pistons transmitted to the crankshaft.
The curves show how torque and power change with engine speed: power depends on both torque and rotational speed.
The two peaks do not necessarily coincide: power also depends on speed and can rise after the torque peak.
The curve shows how torque changes with engine speed: for example, it identifies the range where the engine offers more torque and helps select a gear suited to the load.

The quiz marks this TRUE. For example, the Volvo D13TC provides high torque at low rpm and is designed for efficiency; that does not prove peak efficiency always coincides with peak torque. The optimum depends on engine and load.
The quiz marks this TRUE: an efficient engine speed with sufficient torque can limit fuel use while maintaining speed. The exact trade-off depends on engine, load and route, not just peak-torque rpm.
In typical engine curves the torque peak comes before the power peak: as speed rises, power can continue to increase after torque reaches its maximum.
The characteristic curve relates engine torque output to engine speed, not vehicle weight.
In a typical characteristic curve, torque rises with engine speed to a maximum and then falls; it does not follow the stated minimum.
Torque is the product of the force and its perpendicular lever arm about the axis, not their sum.
The power curve shows power output at different engine speeds, not torque against vehicle dimensions.
On a typical characteristic curve, power rises with engine speed to a maximum and then falls; the exact point depends on the engine.
The curve lets you compare the power available at different engine speeds.

The quiz marks this FALSE. The torque curve alone cannot identify maximum fuel consumption: at the same engine speed, consumption also changes with load. Comparing consumption requires the engine map and a specified measurement.
The typical power curve rises to a maximum and then falls; it does not first reach a minimum as stated.

The quiz marks this TRUE, but the torque curve alone does not show where maximum efficiency occurs. The efficiency map depends on speed and load; checking the stated coincidence requires engine data for the conditions concerned.
On a typical characteristic curve, torque rises to a maximum and then decreases at higher engine speeds.
The two peaks do not necessarily coincide: power depends on both torque and rotational speed and can continue rising after peak torque.
The curves show how available torque and power change with engine speed, describing useful engine characteristics.
Keeping the engine at maximum speed all the time is not a rule for reducing emissions. Efficient driving uses a gear and engine speed suited to conditions.
A properly matched deflector above the cab directs air over the load and reduces the aerodynamic drag of the combination.
Drag increases approximately with the square of speed relative to the air, so an increase in speed produces a more than proportional increase in force.
With coefficient, density and air-relative speed unchanged, increasing frontal area increases drag force proportionally.
A wet road concerns tire contact with the road; aerodynamic drag instead depends on airflow around the vehicle.
Speed matters: other conditions being equal, aerodynamic force rises with the square of speed relative to the air.
Excess load takes more energy to move the vehicle and can increase fuel consumption and emissions; the effect on individual pollutants depends on conditions.
The drag coefficient describes the effect of shape and airflow; it does not directly depend on vehicle weight.
Overcoming air resistance requires engine energy, so reducing it can improve fuel consumption.
The relationship is direct, not inverse: other conditions being equal, a larger frontal area produces more drag.
Aerodynamic force depends on air-relative speed, area, density and coefficient; it is not directly proportional to maximum engine power.
Other conditions being equal, drag force rises with the square of speed relative to the air: doubling that speed quadruples the force.
Aerodynamic force is not directly proportional to weight: it depends instead on area, shape, air and relative speed.
At the same speed, a low gear keeps the engine at higher revs. On level ground, a higher gear generally uses less fuel if the engine can run smoothly in it.
Fuel use also depends on engine speed and load: at the same road speed, changing gear changes engine revs and can change consumption.
A steady speed avoids unnecessary acceleration and braking, which use energy and increase fuel consumption.

Better aerodynamics reduces air resistance and the work required from the engine. This can reduce fuel use and also air pollutants such as nitrogen oxides, depending on the engine and driving conditions.
Running the engine at excessively high revs increases fuel consumption. Shift up when conditions allow.
Frequent gear changes do not themselves save fuel: choose a suitable gear and drive smoothly, avoiding unnecessary shifts and acceleration.
The gearbox is part of the transmission: it changes the ratio by which engine motion reaches the driven wheels.
Gear selection also depends on load. A sufficiently high gear that the engine can sustain smoothly can reduce fuel use.
The stability range is bounded by the engine speeds for maximum torque and maximum power, taken from their respective curves.
The upper boundary is maximum-power speed, not minimum-power speed; the other boundary is maximum-torque speed.
Maximum-torque speed is not a limit that must never be exceeded: uphill the engine can also run above it, within the stability range, in a suitable gear.
By changing the ratio, the gearbox changes the force available at the wheels, allowing it to be matched to the resistance the vehicle encounters.
The stability range concerns engine speeds between maximum torque and maximum power; it does not mean the running engine uses no fuel.
In the stability range the engine can adapt to load changes without necessarily requiring a gear change.
The gearbox changes the ratio between engine and driven-wheel rotation, adapting the speed and torque transmitted.
A gear suited to speed and load can keep engine revs between the speeds of maximum torque and maximum power.
A gradient changes resistance to movement. A suitable gear provides the traction or engine braking needed for the chosen speed.
A wider stability range lets the engine accommodate a larger change in engine speed without changing gear: it is more flexible.
A wider stability range lets the engine accommodate a larger change in engine speed without changing gear: it is more flexible.
On the engine diagram this range runs from maximum-torque speed to maximum-power speed; between them the engine can adapt to changes in load.
On an uphill slope, the component of weight along the slope adds to resistance: more traction is needed to maintain speed.
A higher gear provides less torque multiplication. When appropriate, a lower gear is used to obtain more force at the wheels.
A lower gear multiplies engine torque more, making more force available at the driven wheels.
A higher gear provides less torque multiplication; a lower gear makes more force available at the wheels.
Downhill, the component of weight along the slope helps the vehicle move, so more traction is not needed to overcome the slope; engine braking may be needed to control speed.
The vehicle’s length does not determine tractive force: at a given engine torque, transmission reduction and wheel radius matter.
A high gear provides less torque multiplication; a lower gear increases the force available at the wheels.
A lower gear increases reduction and multiplies the torque delivered to the wheels, increasing the force available.
Low-range gears increase transmission reduction and thus wheel torque and available tractive force.
Low gears multiply engine torque more and make more force available at the wheel rim.
The opposite is true: low gears multiply torque more and increase the tractive force available at the wheels.
To increase wheel force, use a lower gear, which multiplies torque more, rather than a higher one.
On a steep descent, use an appropriate low gear: it increases engine braking and helps control speed.
Other things being equal, greater weight increases rolling resistance and, uphill, the force due to the gradient, so more traction is needed.
More load increases the resistance on the climb. A lower gear, not a higher one, can provide the additional force needed.
Other things being equal, a heavier load increases resistance, especially gradient resistance uphill; more wheel force is needed.
On the same gradient, more load increases resistance to climbing. A lower gear makes more force available at the wheels.
A steeper climb increases gradient resistance. A lower gear multiplies torque more and helps overcome it.
Shifting from third to fourth reduces torque multiplication: at the same engine torque, wheel force falls.
To maintain motion when resistance increases, greater wheel force is needed to balance it.
Wheel force is not constant: the selected gear changes torque multiplication; low gears provide more.
Electronic systems can help avoid a crash, like ABS, or reduce injuries in a crash, like the airbag control unit.
The quiz marks VERO. ABS modulates braking to limit wheel lock and help retain steering. It does not guarantee a shorter total stopping distance; reaction, speed and grip also matter.
ABS acts during braking to prevent wheel lock and help preserve steering; it does not reduce fuel consumption during acceleration.

ACC regulates speed and the gap to the vehicle ahead; ABS instead helps retain steering while braking. ABA can denote emergency brake assistance, sometimes integrated with ACC: the labels are not universal synonyms.

ACC adjusts speed to maintain a set gap to the vehicle ahead within system limits; the driver remains responsible. ABA is not a universal synonym: in some systems it names emergency braking assistance and may include adaptive cruise functions.

In many configurations ACC uses radar to detect the distance and relative speed of the vehicle ahead and adjust speed. It may also use a camera. ABA can mean emergency braking assistance, sometimes integrated with adaptive cruise functions.
ASR limits driven-wheel spin during acceleration; ABS manages wheel lock during braking.
ASR can brake a spinning driven wheel; through the differential this allows more torque to be applied to the other wheel that retains grip.
Traction control is electronic and acts on driven-wheel spin; it is not a purely mechanical device acting on all wheels.
Emergency brake assist increases the available braking force; it does not apply minimum pressure.
Adaptive suspension electronically adjusts damping to driving conditions, balancing road holding and comfort.
Speed is among the inputs adaptive suspension can use to choose damping, so it cannot be ruled out.
ELC regulates suspension height against the desired level, not vehicle acceleration.
Level control can lower the entrance side of a stationary bus, making boarding and alighting easier.
LDWS warns of unintentional lane departure, not every turn at an intersection.
LDWS typically uses a forward-facing camera to recognize lane markings; rear bumper sensors do not describe this function.
ESP compares actual movement with the intended direction and counteracts skidding, helping maintain the path within physical limits.
If actual movement differs from the intended direction, ESP can reduce power and brake individual wheels to counteract a skid.
CBC counters instability when braking in a bend by varying brake pressure between wheels; it does not promote uncontrolled rotation.
When starting uphill, HHC temporarily keeps the brakes applied after pedal release, preventing rollback while the driver moves to the accelerator.
There is no universal 15% gradient threshold for HHC: it can assist on gentler slopes, subject to manufacturer conditions.
CDC continuously adjusts the damping of the shock absorbers according to driving conditions, helping to limit body movement and maintain stability and comfort.
CDC adjusts shock absorber damping force; it does not continuously regulate vehicle acceleration.
APA assists parking, for example by steering into a detected space; ESP stabilizes the path while driving.
Parking sensors can measure distances to obstacles in front of and behind the vehicle; the assistance system uses this information during the maneuver.
EBD distributes braking force according to load and conditions, limiting braking on less-loaded wheels to reduce their risk of locking.
Less-loaded wheels can transmit less braking force: EBD limits their braking rather than automatically assigning them more force.
TPMS monitors pressure and warns with a light or indicator when it detects low pressure. The warning may not be immediate and does not replace regular checks.
Adaptive headlights change beam distribution to suit conditions, improving road illumination and limiting glare for others.
PAX retains the tire on the rim and uses a support ring after pressure loss. Michelin specifies up to about 200 km under stated conditions, far less than 2,000 km.

The quiz marks this FALSE: 200 km/h is not the relevant threshold. Article 1 of EU Regulation 2021/1341 covers M and N vehicles with a maximum design speed above 70 km/h. A vehicle above 200 km/h also exceeds that threshold; this is not the speed at which the system activates.
DDAW assesses alertness by analyzing vehicle systems, such as driving or steering patterns, and warns the driver when needed.
Some ADAS can intervene autonomously: automatic emergency braking can brake when it detects a collision risk. Results depend on conditions and system limits.
A connected vehicle exchanges data with other vehicles or infrastructure directly or through network services: information exchange is the defining feature.
Automated driving extends automation beyond assistance: with assisted systems, the driver continues to monitor the driving task.
Depending on the function, ADAS can adjust speed, brake or intervene in steering; some intervene to avoid or mitigate an imminent danger.
ADAS automate individual assistance functions, while higher levels assign more of the driving task to the system.
ISA is an assistance function: it informs or warns the driver about the speed limit and can help them comply with it.
Driver Alert Control is an aid that warns when driving becomes erratic, for example because of distraction or fatigue.
Drum and disc brakes are two types of friction brake: they use different surfaces to slow the wheel.
Excessive heat can alter the friction material on the shoes, reducing friction and therefore braking effectiveness.
In friction braking, the energy of motion is converted mainly into heat.
The braking surfaces rub together: friction opposes wheel rotation and slows the vehicle.

The quiz marks this FALSE, but the wording does not say that an emergency occurs only without dual wheels. A puncture can also be dangerous with duals: continuing with a flat tyre can overload its mate. Severity depends on pressure loss and driving conditions.
An actuator pushes the shoes against the inside of the drum; friction slows the wheel.
A drum brake uses shoes against the drum; a caliper that presses pads is characteristic of a disc brake.
Both brakes use friction but have different structures: shoes against a drum or pads against a disc.
The drum works with shoes; the caliper is instead a disc-brake component that presses the pads.
The shoes carry friction lining, which is pressed against the drum.
Drum brakes are also used on heavy vehicles; there is no general design incompatibility.
In general, a disc dissipates heat into the air more readily than a drum, helping it cool during braking.
Disc cooling uses air around the disc and, in ventilated discs, internal channels; it does not require a compressor.
Engine braking supplements the service brakes: slowing with the engine reduces the work demanded of disc brakes without replacing them.
The caliper presses the pads against the surfaces of the disc; friction slows the wheel.
Heavy vehicles can also be fitted with disc brakes: their use is not limited to light vehicles.
Excessive heat can cause fade: lining friction decreases and braking becomes less effective.
A ventilated disc has channels that promote airflow and heat dissipation; a drum is more enclosed.
Generally, it is the disc that dissipates heat more readily: the more enclosed drum tends to cool less effectively.
The brake booster assists the driver by amplifying the force applied to the pedal, increasing the action on the braking circuit.
In a hydraulic circuit, the pedal creates pressure in the fluid, which transmits it to the wheel brake cylinders.
The compressor fills reservoirs with compressed air, which the circuit uses to apply the brakes.
Air is compressed and stored in reservoirs before being sent to the brake chambers.
The reservoirs of an air brake system contain compressed air, not oil for braking.
Air pressure acts on the brake chamber diaphragm, which moves the brake linkage.
The antifreeze device introduces vapour into the air to reduce freezing of moisture in the circuit.
The dashboard gauge shows the air pressure in the brake circuit reservoirs.
The oil pressure gauge concerns engine oil pressure; the air brake gauge indicates air pressure.
The air brake gauge indicates the air pressure in the reservoirs, not water pressure.
An abnormal pressure drop shown by the gauge can indicate a fault, such as an air leak.

The quiz marks this TRUE. Gauges show the pressure in the monitored service-brake circuit reservoirs; they may be separate instruments or one gauge with two needles. This does not guarantee an individual reading for every supply or auxiliary tank.
The gauge allows the driver to check air pressure stored in the service circuit reservoirs.
Air is compressible: the compressor pressurizes it and the stored air operates the brakes.
The driver compares the indicated pressure with the operating values specified for the vehicle.
The gauge measures air pressure, not its temperature.
The air gauge monitors pressure in the pneumatic brake circuits, not the operation of the engine cooling system.
The compressor draws in and compresses air to supply the reservoirs; it does not compress oil to operate the brakes.
The compressor draws in air, compresses it and sends it to the system reservoirs.
The compressor receives motion from the engine crankshaft through drive components, for example belts and pulleys or gears.
The compressor is driven by the engine, not by the driveshaft that carries motion toward the wheels.
Spider and side gears belong to the differential. The air compressor typically has pistons that move in cylinders and compress the air.
The air cleaner treats compressed air, removing contaminants such as moisture and oil particles before they reach the circuit.
The gauge indicates air pressure, not the amount of impurities in the reservoir.
The antifreeze device acts on moisture in the circuit air to reduce ice formation, not on oil in a converter.
The air cleaner treats compressed air and its contaminants, not the oil in a converter.
The unit regulates and protects brake air pressure; the gearbox has a separate function.
The governor controls the compressor, loading it at the lower threshold and unloading it at the upper one, restoring pressure when it falls.
The safety valve releases air if pressure becomes excessive, protecting the reservoirs against overpressure.
A check valve lets air flow into the reservoir but prevents it returning toward the source.
One atmosphere is not the reservoirs' structural test pressure: they must withstand pressures well above normal working pressure.
A dedicated compressor compresses the brake air, which is stored in reservoirs; it is not taken from compression in the engine cylinders.
The compressor supplies the reservoirs, which store compressed air for operating the brakes.
The secondary brake must be able to stop the vehicle with a prescribed performance if service braking fails.
In a common dual-circuit system the pedal controls both circuits; if one fails, the other can provide residual secondary braking.
The parking brake warning light tells the driver that the brake is applied, distinguishing it from normal service braking.
The dual brake valve receives air from the reservoirs and meters it to the service circuits when the pedal is pressed; it does not fill the reservoirs.
The dual brake valve is operated by the brake pedal. The manual control is associated with the parking brake.
Pressing the pedal lets the dual brake valve pass air from the reservoirs to the service brake circuits and actuators.
The pedal operates the valve, which varies the pressure sent to the actuators, allowing the driver to modulate braking.
The dual brake valve meters brake air; the transmission differential allows the driven wheels to rotate at different speeds on a bend.
The dual brake valve controls pneumatic brake circuits via the pedal; gearbox type neither determines its function nor imposes that prohibition.
The dual brake valve is operated by the brake pedal and meters air to the circuits; it is not operated by the air-hydraulic converter.
To apply a spring parking brake, the control exhausts air from the spring chamber: the spring supplies the braking force. Air releases it.
The manual control operates the parking brake circuit, controlling pressure in the spring brake chamber.

The quiz marks this FALSE, but does not identify the vehicle or whether the control applies or releases the brake. In spring brakes, air normally compresses the spring to release them; venting the air lets the spring apply them. Which axles have spring brakes depends on the configuration.
The hand valve controls the spring parking brake; the retarder is a separate device.
The driver applies the parking brake with a dedicated manual control, which controls the spring brake circuit.
A spring brake requires compressed air to release it. If pressure is insufficient, the spring keeps it applied and prevents normal departure.
The combined actuator has service and spring sections: the manual control operates the latter, exhausting or admitting air to apply or release the brake.
The automatic load-sensing modulator adjusts braking pressure to the load detected by the vehicle; the driver does not adjust it for the load.
When the vehicle is unladen, the valve reduces brake pressure in proportion to the load, limiting wheel lock. This prevention assumes correctly designed brakes and a dry road.
The valve can sense load through spring deflection or suspension bellows pressure and adjust braking accordingly.
The valve adjusts pressure to the axle brakes according to load: it reduces it when the vehicle is light compared with fully loaded.
The valve adjusts braking pressure to the load; it does not control the height of the loading platform.
The valve adjusts pressure to the load; it does not react to lockup at all brakes. ABS instead uses wheel speed to modulate pressure when wheels risk locking.
The compressor draws in atmospheric air, compresses it and supplies the reservoirs that store it for the pneumatic circuit.
A compressor, for example a piston type, produces the compressed air. Being driven by gears does not make it a gear-type air pump.
Air controlled by the brake moves a piston in the converter, which actuates the hydraulic cylinder and pressurizes the brake fluid.
In an air-over-hydraulic system, the reservoirs supply the brake valve, which controls air to the converters downstream of it.
The converter uses pneumatic force to pressurize hydraulic fluid, which reaches the wheel brake cylinders.
In the converter the hydraulic cylinder is supplied from a brake fluid reservoir; compressed air remains in the pneumatic section.
The converter pressurizes fluid in the hydraulic circuit that operates the wheel brakes, not a lubrication circuit.
Compressed air and brake fluid work in separate sections connected by the converter; they do not form a mixture with water.
The converters link the two sections functionally: air force operates the hydraulic cylinder supplying the brakes.

The quiz marks this FALSE. In an air-over-hydraulic system, compressed air is stored, while hydraulic braking pressure develops when the brake is applied. A small residual pressure may remain; both circuits still need to be checked for correct operation before departure.
The circuit uses a compressor, reservoirs, a valve and converters; a timing chain is not a component of it.
This is not always so: in the air-over-hydraulic layout the pedal valve controls air to the converter, which sends pressurized fluid to the wheel brakes.
The circuit combines a compressed-air section with a hydraulic section: the converter transfers force between them.
The converter uses compressed air to operate the hydraulic brake circuit; it does not select transmission ratios.
The converter receives already compressed air and uses its force to generate hydraulic pressure for the wheel brakes.
The circuit uses a compressed-air supply and a brake fluid reservoir; it has no water tank for operating the brakes.
One or more converters receive air controlled by the brake valve; the pneumatic piston actuates the hydraulic cylinder that sends fluid to the brakes.
The converter operates the hydraulic brakes. The differential allows the driven wheels to travel different distances on a bend and thus rotate at different speeds.
Air pressure acts on the pneumatic piston, which operates the hydraulic piston and produces pressure in the brake fluid.
The pneumatic section stores and controls compressed air; the converter operates the hydraulic section that delivers pressure to the wheel brakes.
Compressed air acts on the converter, which pressurizes the hydraulic fluid sent to the wheel brakes.
The direction is reversed: the converter uses air pressure to produce pressure in the hydraulic brake circuit.
The governor controls the compressor’s air output according to the pressure in the reservoirs.
The air dryer treats compressed air, reducing the moisture that would otherwise enter the air circuit.
The compressor produces the compressed air; the converter uses its force to pressurize hydraulic fluid sent to the brakes.
The hand valve allows braking without using the pedal; in some systems it applies the secondary brake.
The converter transfers the force of compressed air to hydraulic fluid, which reaches and operates the wheel brakes.
The dual brake valve, operated by the pedal, controls air supplied to the service brake circuits.
In this system the hydraulic circuit operates the wheel brakes; it is not a brake acting on the drive shaft.
Air-over-hydraulic operation can apply the service brakes at the wheels to slow and stop the vehicle; it is not merely an auxiliary retarder.
The compressor produces compressed air that is stored in reservoirs and used by the brake circuit.
The compressor is mechanically driven by the engine to supply the air reservoirs.
The reservoirs hold a supply of compressed air for operating the system.
The brake circuit uses its own hydraulic fluid, separate from the oil lubricating the engine.
The converter connects the two sections: compressed air force pressurizes the hydraulic brake fluid.
Hydraulic fluid is only slightly compressible, so it transmits pressure from the converter to the wheel brakes.
The compressor is driven by the engine, not by the drive shaft carrying power to the wheels.
In the converter, compressed air force is transferred to hydraulic fluid that operates the wheel brakes.
The converter is a brake component: it transfers pneumatic force to the hydraulic circuit that operates the wheel brakes.
The system uses compressed air and hydraulic fluid to transmit braking action; water is not the intended operating fluid.
The protection valve lets air flow into the reservoirs and, if a connected circuit fails, prevents the other reservoirs from draining too. This preserves air for the circuits that have not failed.
The circuit combines compressed-air and hydraulic sections: the converter transfers force between them.
In a purely pneumatic brake, air acts on the actuators; a converter is used when there is a hydraulic section.
Compressed air supplies force to the converter operating the hydraulic circuit; it does not cool the brake shoes.
Hydraulic fluid transmits pressure to the wheel braking components; it does not lubricate the tires.
Engine braking and the retarder provide part of the deceleration, reducing the work and heating of the service brakes.
Excessive heat can cause brake fade: braking becomes less effective and more effort is needed to stop.
The retarder supplies part of the braking without wearing the service brakes, so less use also means less wear on the brake shoes.
Engine braking and the retarder help control speed, reducing the work of the service brakes and their risk of overheating.
Part of the slowing occurs without friction on the service brake linings, so they wear less.
Using the engine or retarder for part of the deceleration reduces use and wear of the service brakes.
The service brake stops the vehicle; engine braking and the retarder help control speed and do not replace the brake used to stop.
For an emergency stop, apply the service brake: the retarder is an aid, not a substitute.
Using both aids together does not automatically lock the wheels. On a slippery surface, however, excessive braking torque at the drive wheels can make them slip.
On a long descent the retarder helps maintain speed without continuously using the service brakes, limiting their wear and heating.
In the diesel engine brake considered by the quiz, injection is cut off during braking: the engine absorbs energy instead of providing drive.
Engine braking uses the resistance of the engine driven by the wheels; it does not work by directly braking the drive shaft.
The quiz marks this FALSE: road speed alone does not determine braking effect. Engine rpm and the selected gear also matter; a low gear can produce high rpm even at moderate road speed.
Use the service brake for sudden braking. Engine braking is an aid for slowing down and controlling speed.

The quiz marks this TRUE, but the temperature effect depends on brake type and operating conditions. One exhaust-brake system can assist idle warm-up; a compression-release brake is also designed for prolonged descents without overheating. This does not establish a universal temperature rise.
On a descent, engine braking helps control speed and reduces use of the brakes; there is no need to avoid it for supposed excessive fuel consumption.
The quiz marks this TRUE. At low road speed a low gear can keep engine rpm useful for engine braking, but the effect depends on gear, rpm and system, not road speed alone.
In an exhaust-brake design, a butterfly valve restricts the exhaust and creates back pressure, increasing resistance in the driven engine.

The quiz marks this FALSE: engine braking does not guarantee that engine temperature will not rise. One exhaust-brake system can assist warm-up at idle; downhill behaviour depends on the system and conditions.
On long descents, engine braking helps control speed and reduces the work of the service brakes; it should not be ruled out for fear of damaging it.
ABS detects a wheel tending to lock and automatically modulates braking pressure, helping the wheels keep turning.
ABS is not always optional: it is mandatory for various vehicle categories and type-approval dates.
ABS does not amplify the driver’s force: it controls brake pressure when a wheel tends to lock.
The ABS requirement depends on the vehicle category and applicable type-approval rules; it does not apply indiscriminately to every vehicle already on the road.
The driver applies the brake, while ABS intervenes automatically when sensors detect a risk of wheel lock.
The requirement is not limited to the categories listed: M1 vehicles also have type-approval requirements for ABS. The obligations depend on vehicle type and applicable rules.
Avoiding wheel lock helps preserve steering control and often shortens stopping distance. The surface matters: in some ABS tests on loose gravel, stopping distance increased.
For gradual braking, progressively modulate pedal pressure; repeatedly pressing and releasing it is not what makes braking gradual.
The driver can select retarder operation, for example with a lever or pedal, depending on the vehicle's system.
A retarder cannot be assumed to work best at the lowest possible speed: its effectiveness varies with type and speed and ends when the vehicle stops.
There is no general 80 km/h threshold that activates the retarder: its control depends on the system, for example a lever or brake pedal.
A retarder does not depend on the exhaust for its action: a hydraulic one can act in the transmission, while an electromagnetic one uses induction.
The retarder provides sustained braking alongside the service brakes; alone it does not guarantee a rapid stop when one is needed.
Electromagnetic retarders use induction; hydraulic retarders create resistance using fluid.

The quiz marks this TRUE. In some configurations the retarder does not operate at low speed and the service brake is needed to stop; effectiveness depends on the type and speed, and other models also work at low speed.
Using a retarder does not necessarily cut off the diesel supply: it is an auxiliary braking device, separate from engine fuel control.
Inertia depends on mass, not on whether the road rises or falls. The slope instead changes gravity's effect on motion.
A low gear increases engine braking and slows the vehicle; to use its existing momentum, choose an appropriate gear without making the engine struggle.
When fully loaded, the vehicle has more mass and therefore more inertia: more force is needed to produce the same change in motion.

The quiz marks this TRUE. More precisely, with a suitable gear engaged, the whole vehicle’s momentum drives the engine and transmission: on modern vehicles, releasing the accelerator often cuts fuel until engine speed falls low. Slowing this way can also reduce brake use.
Greater inertia does not by itself shorten stopping distance: it means greater resistance to changing motion. Distance also depends on braking force and grip.
By anticipating a stop, the driver can release the accelerator and let the vehicle advance using its existing motion, braking when necessary.
The quiz marks this TRUE and uses “force” informally. In physics, inertia is the property by which a body resists changes in speed or direction; it is not an extra braking force.
The duplex valve controls the two brake circuits; overloading does not automatically prevent it from working, although it compromises vehicle safety and performance.
The remaining circuit provides emergency braking; it does not permit normal continued driving. Stop safely and have the brake fault repaired.
A break in a pipe supplied by the reservoir can release air and rapidly lower the indicated pressure in the affected circuit.
The governor controls air pressure: if the control or a protection valve malfunctions, pressure can exceed its intended value.
The compressor supplies air to the reservoirs; a fault can prevent it from restoring sufficient system pressure.
Check for sufficient pressure before moving off, not necessarily before starting the engine: the compressor may need the engine running to charge the system.
In separated circuits, protection prevents a leak in one from emptying the other, which retains secondary braking capability. The fault still needs repair.
The secondary brake can stop the vehicle if the service brake fails; it may use the part of the system that remains operational.
A retarder does not repair a pressure fault or replace the service brake. Stop safely and have the system checked.
A working circuit can provide residual braking, but the system is faulty. Stop safely as soon as possible and have it checked.
The pressure gauge shows reservoir pressure. Comparing its reading with the normal range can reveal excessive pressure too.
Pressing the pedal consumes air rather than filling the reservoirs. The compressor restores pressure; if it does not recover, have the fault checked.
The dual brake valve controls service braking. Raising engine speed does not repair it: stop safely and have the fault checked.
The governor controls the compressor to keep pressure within its limits. A fault can prevent charging from stopping and cause excess pressure.

The quiz marks this TRUE: speed limiters are required for the relevant M2, M3, N2 and N3 categories. The rules also distinguish vehicles by registration date and contain specific exclusions; “all” does not remove those conditions.

The quiz marks this TRUE: trucks over 3.5 tonnes fall within N2 or N3, categories covered by speed-limiter rules. Registration dates and specified exclusions also matter, so weight alone is not sufficient.
For these vehicles mass alone is not enough: the speed limiter provisions also specify registration dates and conditions of application.
The date alone is not enough: the requirement also depends on the vehicle category and mass and other applicable conditions.
A speed limiter is also mandatory for categories N2 and N3 under the applicable conditions; it is not merely recommended.
Gear ratios adapt engine speed and wheel force to vehicle speed and the resistance to overcome, which varies with gradient, load and air.
Minimum torque is not the reference. To save fuel, select the gear that keeps the engine in its specified efficient range.
A low gear increases engine braking and helps control speed without relying continuously on the service brakes.
At the same engine torque, a low gear multiplies wheel torque more than a high gear, providing greater tractive force.
Climbing, especially when loaded, may require a low gear: the higher ratio helps produce more force at the wheels.
A low gear multiplies wheel torque more, providing more force to overcome the resistance of a loaded climb.
In a low gear the wheels turn the engine faster: its resistance helps slow the vehicle downhill.
A low gear promotes engine braking and helps contain downhill speed; it does not in itself increase braking distance.
For economical driving, aim for the engine’s efficient speed range, choosing a gear suited to conditions without compromising control.
The tachometer’s optimal range helps select a gear that keeps the engine efficient while dealing with the effort of the climb.
The gear ratio changes engine speed, not the vehicle’s aerodynamic shape. The drag coefficient does not simply fall when a higher gear is selected.
If engine speed leaves the optimal range, changing gear helps return it to the useful range and maintain the traction needed uphill.
Downhill, a low gear uses engine resistance to help contain and stabilize speed; the brakes remain available when needed.
A low gear increases engine braking, so the service brakes are used less and the brake pads wear less.
Downshifting raises engine speed at the same road speed, bringing it back toward the useful range instead of leaving it too far below peak torque speed.
A low gear increases engine braking, helping control downhill speed and reducing reliance on the service brakes.
A high gear suited to the road speed generally keeps engine speed and fuel consumption down, provided the engine is not labouring.
A steeper gradient does not necessarily call for a high gear: a lower gear may be needed for pulling power uphill or engine braking downhill.
To use engine braking on a long descent, select a sufficiently low gear before starting down, rather than a higher one.
The economy band on the tachometer helps identify an operating speed that favours lower fuel consumption in normal conditions.
On a steeper gradient, a lower gear can provide more driving force at the wheels uphill or more engine braking downhill.
A higher gear would reduce engine speed further; downshifting brings it back toward the useful operating range.
A loaded vehicle may need a lower gear on a climb to provide the necessary pulling force; shifting up is not always appropriate.
The limit does not apply only to rear wheels. For Italian autoveicoli, including cars and trucks, as well as trolleybuses and trailers, the main grooves must be at least 1.6 mm deep on all wheels.
Tire pressure can fall over time: checking it periodically with a gauge helps maintain the recommended value.
Different pressures on the same axle can produce uneven handling and cause the vehicle to drift from a straight path.
The correct pressure can vary with load. Follow the manufacturer’s values for the load and operating conditions.
For dual tires too, use the pressure specified for that configuration and load, not an arbitrarily lower pressure.
An annual check is not enough: pressure should be checked periodically because it can fall even without visible damage.
Before departure, inspect the tires for damage, wear or signs of pressure loss that require attention.
The reference pressure is measured cold: heat after driving raises the reading and can make the comparison misleading.
Before departure, check that the tires do not look flat; use a gauge to check the correct pressure.
Underinflated dual tires can deform until they touch: friction between the sidewalls can damage them.
Low pressure does not reduce the risk of hydroplaning: it can promote loss of road contact on water, especially as speed increases.
Pressure that is too low can increase wear on the tread shoulders instead of distributing it evenly.
Low pressure tends to wear the shoulders most; centre wear is typically associated with excessive pressure.
An unbalanced wheel can cause vibration and irregular tread wear; balancing corrects the imbalance.
With excessive pressure, the centre can carry more load and wear faster than the edges.
Excess pressure tends to wear the center of the tread; shoulder wear is typical of insufficient pressure.
Slip angle is the angle between the direction the wheel points and the direction it travels, not an angle between two vehicle axles.

The periodic inspection checks tire condition and wear, among other things. Tire slip angle arises while driving under lateral force and is not a measurement specified in the periodic tire inspection.
Greater rear than front slip characterizes oversteer: the rear tends to move toward the outside of the bend, rather than reducing that tendency.
In oversteer the vehicle takes a tighter turn, but the rear wheels have the greater slip angle. Greater front slip instead characterizes understeer.
Slip arises from the tire's elastic response to lateral cornering forces and can occur even on a well-maintained vehicle. Maintenance does not eliminate it.

The quiz marks this FALSE. Excessive understeer with loss of front grip can widen the path and reduce control. Mild understeer designed into a vehicle in its normal operating range is a different meaning and can make its response more predictable.
In an understeering vehicle, increasing speed in a bend increases the lateral force required, so more steering is needed to maintain the same path.
When front slip exceeds rear slip, the front follows a wider path than the turn requested: this is understeer.
In oversteer the rear tends to move outward and the vehicle rotates more than intended; if severe, it can spin.
In oversteer the vehicle turns more than intended and the rear tends outward. Turning less than intended is understeer.
Ineffective shock absorbers can alter wheel contact and response. In some conditions, particularly with a front defect, the vehicle can become more prone to understeer.
In oversteer rear slip exceeds front slip: the rear tends outward and the vehicle takes a tighter turn than intended.
Running wide is typical of understeer. In oversteer, the rear tends outward and the vehicle turns more than intended.
Slip angle is related to lateral force and tire deformation in a bend; it does not arise solely from driving force or only on driven front wheels.
A rear load does not always increase understeer: by changing tire response, it can also shift the vehicle toward oversteer.
Pressure changes tire deformation and its response to lateral forces, so it also affects slip angle in a bend.
In understeer the front deviates more than the rear and the vehicle follows a wider curve than the steering input calls for.
If the rear wheels have more slip than the front wheels, the rear tends outward and the vehicle turns more than intended: this is oversteer.
In a bend, lateral force deforms the tire and its actual direction of travel differs from its orientation. This difference is the slip angle.
In oversteer the rear tends outward and the vehicle turns more than intended. Load distribution can contribute to changing this behavior.
Pressure affects tire deformation and lateral response, and therefore slip angle too: the angle is not independent of pressure.
Understeer does not cancel slip: it describes behavior in which the front wheels have greater slip than the rear wheels.

The quiz marks this FALSE, but slope alone does not always predict understeer: the vehicle, load and grip matter. Under some steady uphill conditions, rearward load transfer can instead increase the tendency to understeer.
In understeer the front tends to run wide, so the vehicle turns less than requested by the steering input.
Greater front slip makes the vehicle follow a wider curve than intended.
Lateral force deforms the tire, making its direction of travel differ from its orientation.
Axle load affects the tires’ lateral behavior and therefore their slip; slip is not independent of load.
Power steering assists steering; its presence does not imply greater tire slip.
If the rear slips more than the front, the vehicle turns more than intended and tends to tighten its path.
It is the angle between the direction the tire points and the direction in which it actually travels.
Pressure changes a tire’s cornering stiffness and can therefore affect its tendency to understeer.
Load changes the tire’s lateral response and can therefore change its slip in a turn.
In a turn, lateral force deforms the tire, including its carcass; this compliance contributes to slip.

The quiz marks this TRUE. Camber changes deformation of the contact patch and the tyre’s lateral response, affecting cornering behaviour. The wording does not necessarily establish sidewall rupture or structural collapse; its precise meaning here is unclear.
Understeer makes the vehicle turn less than intended; in oversteer the rear tends to swing outward.
If the rear tires slip more than the front, the tail tends to slide outward; in extreme cases the vehicle can spin.
The tire does not travel exactly in the direction it points: lateral force deforms it and produces the difference.
If the tail slides outward, countersteering points the wheels toward the intended path to help regain control.
A temporary turn outward is countersteering: it helps point the wheels toward the intended path as the rear slides.
Accelerating without correcting the steering is not a recovery rule: point the wheels toward the intended path and adjust the throttle to the situation.
Hard braking can worsen the rear loss of grip; correct the direction smoothly instead.
If excess acceleration makes the driven rear wheels slip, easing off the accelerator helps restore grip and directional control.
In oversteer the rear moves outward: countersteer toward the intended path rather than adding steering into the turn.
Countersteering points the wheels toward the intended path as the rear slides; adjust it as the vehicle regains grip.
In understeer the vehicle follows a wider, not tighter, curve than the driver intends.
In understeer the path widens relative to the steering input: the vehicle turns less than intended.

The quiz marks this TRUE, but does not specify the condition. In steady understeer, while the front tyres retain grip, more steering angle may be needed to follow a curve. If the front tyres are already skidding, do not add steering: smoothly reduce speed and steering input to regain grip.
To regain directional control, coordinate steering and throttle: ease off the accelerator and point the wheels toward the intended path without excessive steering.
Hard braking is not the required correction: regain grip and directional control with smooth inputs.
ITS apply information and communication technology to transport management, connecting data, vehicles and infrastructure to support the system’s activities.
ITS can warn of hazards and assist drivers, helping prevent crashes and protect people.
Location and cargo information help operators follow vehicles and goods during a journey and detect irregularities.
ITS also support efficiency: traffic information and fleet management help organize passenger and freight movements.
Vehicle locations and traffic information help a fleet manager track vehicles and plan more efficient routes.

The quiz marks this FALSE, but “desires and passions” is vague and does not rule out personalized choices. Telematics services can provide traffic information and alternative routes, helping a driver assess the journey.
ADAS assist driving according to detected conditions: for example, they warn of a possible collision or help keep the vehicle in its lane.
ATMS manage traffic across a network: for example, they can use detection and controllers to adapt traffic signals to flows.
ATIS provide travelers with information, such as traffic and travel times, which can guide their choice of route.
Demand management concerns choices such as travel time, route or mode; assistance with driving maneuvers is the role of ADAS.
ADAS assist driving maneuvers, for example by warning of collisions; traveler information systems provide information for choosing a route.
Pricing and quantity restrictions are possible tools for managing transport demand, not approaches that must necessarily be abandoned.
In some schemes, travelers can earn credits for sustainable mobility and trade them: these are travel incentives, not driving licences.
Knowing the location of goods, traffic, schedules and availability helps coordinate transfers between modes and reduce waiting.
Automated handling at terminals can facilitate transfers of goods between modes and make operations smoother.
Remote monitoring can provide the location and condition of goods during a journey, information especially useful for dangerous goods.
Automatic positioning determines where a moving object is: for example, it can track a vehicle or shipment through a logistics network.
Automatic positioning helps manage freight fleets: knowing where vehicles are helps operators track and organize their movements.
Automatic identification associates a readable code with a unit or travel credential, allowing the system to recognize it and connect it with relevant data.
Automatic identification can link a code to relevant data, for example about a load unit or travel credential; it does not exclude such information.
A barcode on a travel credential can be read automatically and linked to passenger data; for example, two-dimensional codes are used on boarding passes.
Automatic identification also serves to check and verify units: scanning can record which packages were unloaded.
An identifier read on goods can link the physical unit to related electronic messages, making it easier to associate documents.
Sensors embedded in the road are not the only option: devices above the road, such as microwave sensors, can also detect traffic.
Inductive loops embedded in the pavement detect vehicles; microwave, infrared and ultrasonic sensors can also collect traffic data.
Loops can also detect length and axles: suitable configurations and processing equipment derive these details as the vehicle passes.
Diagnosis describes the present state, for example using speed or congestion levels; forecasting concerns future conditions.
To inform users about current conditions, traffic data must first be collected and processed to describe what they will encounter.
Forecasting concerns the future; identifying the present situation is the task of diagnosis.
Not all statistical methods require complex, lengthy calculations: for example, a forecast can use the average of recent observations. The computational workload depends on the method chosen.
By identifying the same vehicle at two points, the system compares passage times: their difference gives that vehicle’s travel time over the section.
A model can represent abnormal events such as a crash and estimate their effects on the network. Reliability depends on the data, calibration and representation of the scenario.
Simulation needs careful calibration against local data; it cannot be assumed to be always fast or that default parameters suffice.
The algorithm automatically analyzes sensor data and flags a possible anomaly, allowing an incident to be identified quickly without waiting for an operator to notice it.
Early detection helps start the response and inform users sooner, potentially limiting queues and risks associated with the incident.
Prompt, reliable detection allows verification and response to begin sooner, helping remove obstructions; it does not guarantee their removal on its own.

Detecting an incident early allows the response to start sooner. Reducing missed events and false alarms helps ensure real incidents are not overlooked and resources are not wasted; automatic alerts do not depend on a human call.
Data quality and sensor coverage affect the ability to detect events: inaccurate data or sensors too far apart can worsen performance.
Within ITS, advanced traffic management uses network data and controls, while advanced information makes them useful to travelers. These functions complement each other.
Sensors collect data, for example on flows, incidents or environmental conditions, which the system uses to monitor and manage the network.
Advanced management also includes surveillance: detectors and cameras observe the network and inform management decisions.
Ramp access control is one possible application: signals meter vehicles entering the motorway.
Lane signals can communicate openings, closures and other information to users, integrating control and information.
Ramp control meters entering vehicles to manage flow and congestion; it does not check toll receipts.
When a lane is closed or conditions change, dynamic signs warn drivers and guide them toward available lanes.
Dynamic control uses directions to drivers, such as signs showing open or closed lanes, to regulate flow.
Dynamic control adjusts signal timing to current data; a sequence and durations fixed from historical data describe a preprogrammed plan.
Management can temporarily reserve space for public transport, allowing it to bypass some queues and reduce delays.
In the ideal model, with equal grip and braking proportional to weight, braking force also grows with mass, so mass cancels out. In practice brakes, tires and load also matter.
At the same deceleration, braking distance increases with the square of speed: doubling speed makes it four times as long. Reaction distance is excluded.
For the same mass and constant braking force, braking distance rises with the square of speed: doubling speed makes it four times as long.
At the same initial speed and constant braking force, a larger mass has more inertia and energy to dissipate, so it needs more distance to stop.
At the same initial speed and constant braking force, a larger mass has more kinetic energy and needs more distance to stop.
In a tunnel the prescribed exterior lights, including dipped headlights, are required; there is no requirement to switch on every cab interior light.
Before entering, learn the tunnel’s specific provisions, such as access restrictions, speed and separation: this lets you enter and travel in accordance with that tunnel’s rules.

Pedestrians and cyclists need lateral space. When overtaking cyclists, the road code requires at least 1.5 metres where road conditions permit, as well as a distance appropriate to speed and vehicle size.
There is no general rule requiring heavy vehicles always to use the left lane in a roundabout. They may use the right lane, respecting signs and the conditions of the maneuver.
Wheelbase affects the wheels’ path and overhang affects the space occupied by the ends of the vehicle: both matter when judging the space needed to turn.
The rear wheel cannot mount the sidewalk simply because the vehicle is moving slowly. Plan the turn with its path and the available space in mind.
The distance between the two axles is the wheelbase. Overhang is the part of the vehicle extending beyond an axle toward the front or rear end.
Rear overhang measures how far the vehicle extends behind the rear axle, to its rearmost point.
A length over seven meters does not require moving to the left side. To turn right, stay as close as possible to the right edge and maneuver without creating danger.
Waiting until the area is clear helps the driver complete the turn with enough room, without endangering or obstructing other road users.
At a change of gradient, rear contact risk depends particularly on rear overhang and its ground clearance; front overhang does not measure how far the tail projects. Ramp geometry matters too.
At the same ground clearance, a longer tail behind the rear axle reduces the departure angle and can touch the ground at a change of slope.

The quiz marks this FALSE: as the front rises, the tail can move down toward the ground. Rear overhang, its clearance and the gradient matter; wheelbase is the distance between the axles. Wheelbase can affect the vehicle’s pitch, but its length alone does not establish an increased risk.
At the same ground clearance, greater rear overhang reduces the departure angle and increases the risk of the tail touching the ground when entering the ramp.
A longer rear overhang alone does not determine an increase in understeer: cornering behavior also depends on load distribution and tire characteristics.
If the obstacle prevents vehicles from passing and makes it impossible to stay near the right edge, the obstructed driver must stop and let oncoming traffic through.
The obstructed driver does not have priority: if passing is impossible and they cannot stay near the right edge, they must stop and let oncoming vehicles through.
Roadworks do not give priority to the obstructed driver: if passing is impossible and they cannot stay near the right edge, they must stop and let the others through.
If roadworks prevent passing and make it impossible to stay near the right edge, the obstructed driver must stop and let oncoming vehicles through.
As a rule, the vehicle going downhill stops, not the one going uphill. If the uphill driver has a passing place and reversing would otherwise be necessary, they must stop there.
The uphill driver must stop in the available passing place if the road is so narrow that reversing would otherwise be necessary.
As a rule, the downhill driver stops and pulls right or uses a passing place. If the uphill driver has a passing place and reversing would otherwise be necessary, the uphill driver stops.
The uphill driver must stop in the lay-by if otherwise the narrow road would require reversing.
When reversing is necessary, the vehicle up to 3.5 tonnes normally gives way to the one over 3.5 tonnes. The separate priority of vehicle combinations over other categories must also be considered.
When reversing is necessary, a vehicle combination has priority over other vehicles, so the bus reverses.
When reversing is necessary, the bus has priority over the truck, which must reverse.
Between vehicles in the same category, the downhill vehicle normally reverses, unless it is clearly easier for the uphill vehicle to do so.
When reversing is necessary, the vehicle combination has priority, so the passenger car reverses.
Between vehicles in the same category, the downhill vehicle normally reverses, not the uphill one; an exception applies if it is clearly easier for the uphill vehicle.
This is not an arbitrary choice: between vehicles in the same category the downhill vehicle normally reverses, unless it is clearly easier for the uphill vehicle.
When reversing is necessary, the vehicle up to 3.5 tonnes normally gives way to the one over 3.5 tonnes. The separate priority of vehicle combinations over other categories must also be considered.
The passenger car reverses when necessary: the vehicle combination has priority over other vehicles.
The bus reverses when necessary: the vehicle combination has priority over other vehicles.
The truck reverses when necessary: the bus has priority over it.
Anyone involved in a crash linked to their own conduct must stop and provide their details, as well as any necessary assistance.
The necessary assistance is for people who have been injured, not just passengers in one’s own vehicle.
An injured person needs help: whoever finds them must provide the necessary assistance or immediately notify the authorities.
Emergency responders need to know the substance involved to choose appropriate measures; during ADR transport, inform them of all available details when safe and practicable.
Even without injuries, a dangerous goods spill can create an emergency and require emergency responders.
Warning others of danger and making traffic safe helps prevent further crashes, within the limits of what can be done safely.

The quiz marks this TRUE, but force majeure is not an exhaustive list of possible legal grounds excluding liability. A road user involved in a crash attributable to their conduct must stop and assist. If a genuine impediment prevents direct intervention, call emergency services when it is possible and safe.
The danger or obstruction must be signaled and the road authority or police informed: the rule does not depend on the time of day.
There is no minimum number of injured people: even a dangerous goods spill with no injuries can require an emergency response.
The value of property does not remove the duty to provide necessary assistance to people injured in a crash linked to one’s conduct.
You do not need to have passed a course to help: someone who finds an injured person can provide necessary assistance or immediately notify the authorities.
Before intervening, assess the safety of the scene: exposing yourself to danger can create more casualties and hinder rescue.
Do not give an unconscious person anything to drink: liquid can enter the airway.
A fracture calls for keeping the limb still, not tightening a tourniquet around it. A tourniquet controls severe bleeding; it does not immobilize a fracture.
First make the scene safe and call emergency services if needed; contacting a lawyer is not the first action.
Do not give medicines at random: they may be unsuitable. Call emergency services and follow their instructions.
For a serious eye injury, protect the eye without pressing on an embedded object and await medical help. Small superficial particles may be treated differently.
Do not try to pull an embedded object out of the eye: this can cause further injury. Small superficial particles can instead be flushed with clean water.
An injury or sudden illness may need medical assessment. If the person is at risk, call emergency services and describe their condition.
The priority is to make the scene safe and call emergency services if needed. Contact the insurer afterward, not before every other action.
Do not pull an embedded object out with improvised tools: this may worsen the injury. Protect the eye without pressure and seek help.
Staying calm helps you communicate clearly with emergency services and follow their instructions.
Simply leaving the eye exposed does not protect a serious injury. Protect it without pressing on an embedded object and seek medical help.

The quiz marks this FALSE, but does not specify the type of foreign object. A small loose superficial particle can be gently rinsed with clean water; if an object is embedded or has penetrated the eye, do not try to remove it and seek urgent assistance.
The horn alone is not enough: warn approaching traffic and call emergency services when needed.
Do not give alcohol to a person in shock. Call emergency services and give no drinks while waiting.
A clean dressing can protect a serious eye injury; if an object is embedded, do not press on it.
Checking hazards such as traffic and fire helps prevent further casualties. Act only if it is safe and call the necessary emergency services.
Do not give alcohol to an injured or ill person. If shock is suspected, give no food or drink; seek help and follow the emergency responders’ instructions.
If the injured person cannot be moved, warn approaching traffic and protect the scene without exposing yourself to further danger.
Do not automatically move a trauma casualty: movement can worsen injuries. Move them if essential because of immediate danger.
Smoke or flames indicate danger to casualties and rescuers. Assess the scene from a safe position and call emergency services.
The person should not rub or touch the injured eye: this could worsen the injury. Seek medical help according to its severity.
Do not try to pull an embedded object out of the eye: this can cause further harm. A small superficial particle can instead be flushed with clean water.
Staying with and reassuring the person helps while waiting for emergency services; monitor their condition and notify the dispatcher if it worsens.
On a motorway, waiting for a service vehicle is not enough: reach a safe place and contact the appropriate emergency service.
Warning approaching traffic reduces the risk of further collisions and protects casualties and rescuers.
Do not remove an object embedded in a wound: removal can increase bleeding. Protect the area around it and seek help.
A person involved in an accident connected to their conduct must stop and provide necessary assistance to injured people, including calling emergency services.
It is the immediate help given after sudden illness or injury while awaiting organized emergency assistance.
Actions must be appropriate: improper intervention can worsen injuries. Call emergency services and follow their instructions to help prevent further harm.
First check safety, assess the person and call emergency services; asking for documents is not the first action.
Assistance is also a legal duty: for example, someone finding an injured person must provide necessary assistance or promptly notify the authorities.
It includes simple, prompt actions, such as applying pressure to severe bleeding while awaiting help.
A member of the public can call for help and provide simple care they know how to perform, avoiding actions that could worsen injuries.
It is not reserved for healthcare professionals: bystanders can call emergency services and act within their abilities.
Written consent is not needed to call emergency services or give first aid. If the person is conscious, ask permission before examining or assisting them.
A witness can also provide first aid, for example by calling emergency services and following their instructions.

Movement can worsen a traumatic injury. Avoid moving the injured person unnecessarily and call emergency services. If movement is needed for safety or lifesaving care, such as CPR or control of severe bleeding, follow the dispatcher’s instructions immediately.

A request alone does not require moving them. Avoid moving the injured person unnecessarily and call emergency services. If movement is needed for safety or lifesaving care, such as CPR or control of severe bleeding, follow the dispatcher’s instructions immediately.

When the person cannot move, take particular care not to worsen an injury. Avoid moving the injured person unnecessarily and call emergency services. If movement is needed for safety or lifesaving care, such as CPR or control of severe bleeding, follow the dispatcher’s instructions immediately.

There is no need to wait for police when urgent care is required. Avoid moving the injured person unnecessarily and call emergency services. If movement is needed for safety or lifesaving care, such as CPR or control of severe bleeding, follow the dispatcher’s instructions immediately.

Intoxication does not prohibit necessary movement. Avoid moving the injured person unnecessarily and call emergency services. If movement is needed for safety or lifesaving care, such as CPR or control of severe bleeding, follow the dispatcher’s instructions immediately.

Medical personnel can manage movement, but lifesaving care must not be unnecessarily delayed until they arrive. Avoid moving the injured person unnecessarily and call emergency services. If movement is needed for safety or lifesaving care, such as CPR or control of severe bleeding, follow the dispatcher’s instructions immediately.
Do not automatically remove the helmet immediately: removal can move the head and neck. Do so only if essential and follow emergency services’ instructions.
Do not cover the face: breathing must be checked and the airway kept clear. Call emergency services and follow their instructions.
An unconscious person cannot respond to a request to move their legs. The priorities are calling for help and checking breathing.
Being conscious does not rule out internal injuries or bleeding, which may not be immediately evident after trauma.
Checking responsiveness and breathing helps identify an immediate threat to life and communicate the person’s condition to emergency services.
If the adult is unresponsive, call emergency services immediately and check breathing while the call connects. If breathing is absent or abnormal, start CPR following the dispatcher’s instructions.
Loss of consciousness requires urgent help: 118 activates medical assistance; 112 can also be called.

The quiz marks this TRUE. Current guidance for a lay rescuer helping an unresponsive adult is to call emergency services immediately and check breathing while the call connects, without delaying help to search for a pulse. If breathing is absent or abnormal, start CPR following the dispatcher’s instructions.

An unresponsive person should not automatically be moved. Avoid moving the injured person unnecessarily and call emergency services. If movement is needed for safety or lifesaving care, such as CPR or control of severe bleeding, follow the dispatcher’s instructions immediately.
Consciousness indicates brain activity and circulation at that moment, but does not guarantee adequate breathing or circulation. Both still need assessment.
Assess consciousness by looking for a response to voice and stimuli, not recall of a licence plate: a person can respond while confused.

A blocked airway prevents airflow. If the person is unresponsive and not breathing normally, call emergency services and begin CPR without delay. Remove only visible, easily reached obstructions; do not sweep blindly.

The quiz marks this FALSE, but does not specify the injury. Being conscious alone does not make a coordinated limb test necessary in every case; neurological assessment can be useful in particular situations. After trauma, avoid unnecessary movement and follow emergency-service instructions.
Regaining consciousness does not rule out injury or deterioration. After a loss of consciousness, call emergency services and keep monitoring the person.
Unconsciousness alone does not require tying the person to sticks. Limit movement if trauma is suspected and prioritise airway and breathing, following emergency responders’ instructions.
An answer to questions shows that the person responds to voice. Consciousness may still be impaired, so also check breathing and general condition.

Airway, breathing and circulation are priorities. Do not delay CPR to check a pulse: if the person is unresponsive and not breathing normally, call emergency services and start CPR following the dispatcher.
Being conscious does not mean the person is out of danger. Give necessary assistance, call emergency services and stay to monitor them unless you must leave to summon help.
Consciousness requires circulation and oxygenation, but does not prove that breathing is normal or adequate. Assess breathing and monitor the person.
Speaking to the person and observing their reaction helps assess consciousness. A response to voice does not rule out other injuries.

Rescue breaths provide air when breathing stops. If the person is unresponsive and not breathing normally, call emergency services and start CPR following the dispatcher. For an adult, begin compressions and add rescue breaths if trained; for a child, a rescuer trained in paediatric CPR begins with five rescue breaths.

If the person is unresponsive and not breathing normally, call emergency services and start CPR following the dispatcher. For an adult, begin compressions and add rescue breaths if trained; for a child, a rescuer trained in paediatric CPR begins with five rescue breaths.
Chest movement helps identify breathing. Current guidance is to look at the chest, listen and feel for air; placing a hand on the chest is not essential.

The tongue can obstruct the airway: opening it with a chin lift and gentle head tilt helps air pass. Remove only visible, easily reached objects, without a blind sweep. If the person is unresponsive and not breathing normally, call emergency services and start CPR immediately. If a neck injury is suspected, minimize neck movement; opening the airway remains the priority.
A gentle head tilt with chin lift helps open the airway. If a neck injury is suspected, limit movement and follow the emergency responders’ instructions. Opening the airway remains the priority.
Listening near the mouth and nose helps detect airflow; also watch the chest and feel for breath. Isolated gasps are not normal breathing.
Feeling air on the skin can help assess breathing. Current guidance uses the cheek near the mouth and nose, together with watching the chest and listening; a hand under the nose is not essential.
You do not need to wait for a professional: a first aider can watch the chest and listen and feel for breathing while calling for help.
A chest rising and falling is a sign to look for when assessing breathing; also listen and feel for air to assess whether breathing is normal.
Raising the legs does not restore breathing. If the person is unresponsive and not breathing normally, call emergency services and start CPR immediately.
Throwing water on the face does not restore breathing. If the person is unresponsive and not breathing normally, call emergency services and start CPR immediately.
An uninjured-looking chest does not prove the person is breathing. Watch for it to rise and fall, while also listening and feeling for airflow.

For CPR the person is normally on their back; opening the airway with a gentle head tilt and chin lift helps airflow. If a neck injury is suspected, limit movement and follow emergency responders. Opening the airway remains the priority.

Loosening tight clothing may reduce constriction, but does not replace CPR. If the person is unresponsive and not breathing normally, call emergency services and start CPR immediately, following the dispatcher.

Do not use a jet from a compressed-air system: it can cause serious injury. If the person is unresponsive and not breathing normally, call 112 and start CPR following the dispatcher; rescue breaths use a controlled technique.
You do not need to have taken a course to watch for chest movement and check breathing. If the person is unresponsive and not breathing normally, call 112 and follow the dispatcher’s instructions.

Violent shaking is not resuscitation. Speak to the person and use a gentle touch to check for a response; limit movement if trauma is suspected. If they are unresponsive and not breathing normally, call 112 and begin CPR following the dispatcher.
Do not try to stand the person up: someone who is unresponsive and not breathing normally needs immediate emergency help and resuscitation, following the dispatcher’s instructions.
Rescue breaths deliver air into the lungs. During resuscitation, a trained rescuer can alternate them with chest compressions.
The purpose of rescue breaths is to deliver oxygen-containing air to the lungs, not to administer carbon dioxide.

Rescue breaths provide oxygen when breathing has stopped. If the person is unresponsive and not breathing normally, call 112 and start CPR following the dispatcher. For an adult, begin compressions and add breaths if trained; for a child, a rescuer trained in paediatric CPR starts with five rescue breaths.
Artificial respiration delivers air to the lungs to support oxygenation; it does not mechanically stimulate the whole body.
Giving a drink does not help breathing; never give an unconscious person a drink. If they are not breathing normally, call 112 and follow the dispatcher’s instructions.
Rescue breaths deliver air containing oxygen to the lungs, supporting oxygenation when the person is not breathing normally.
Defibrillator pads are used to analyze the rhythm and deliver a shock if indicated. Artificial respiration instead delivers air into the lungs.
In mouth-to-mouth breathing, the rescuer takes a normal breath and blows into the person’s mouth, watching for the chest to rise. This is a rescue breathing technique.
A carotid pulse can give a healthcare professional a sign of circulation. For lay rescuers, guidelines focus on recognizing unresponsiveness and absent or abnormal breathing without delaying CPR.
Cardiac massage consists of chest compressions; rescue breaths are the separate breathing component of resuscitation.
Compressions are not used in every emergency: they are needed when cardiac arrest is suspected, for example if the person is unresponsive and not breathing normally.
Pricking a finger is not a way to assess the heartbeat. A healthcare professional may check the pulse; a rescuer checks responsiveness and breathing and follows the dispatcher.

In adult CPR, a trained rescuer can alternate compressions and rescue breaths; otherwise perform compressions following the dispatcher. For a child, the paediatric sequence starts with five rescue breaths for a trained rescuer.
Compressions are applied in the center of the chest, on the lower half of the breastbone: they help keep blood circulating during cardiac arrest.
The capillaries in the eye cannot establish whether the heart is beating. A healthcare professional may check the pulse; a rescuer checks responsiveness and breathing and follows the dispatcher.

The carotid pulse can be checked while the head is kept tilted to open the airway. Suspected head or neck injury requires special care; a lay rescuer follows the dispatcher and does not delay CPR to look for a pulse.
Compressions are applied to the breastbone in the center of the chest, not to the carotid artery: they help keep blood circulating.
Chest compressions help maintain blood circulation during cardiac arrest until emergency help arrives.
