High blood pressure does not rule out resuscitation for suspected cardiac arrest. If the person is unresponsive and not breathing normally, call emergency services and start CPR following the dispatcher.
A blow to the head can cause serious brain injury. Changes in consciousness, vomiting or confusion require attention and urgent assessment.
Do not give alcohol after a head injury: it can mask signs of deterioration and make them harder to recognise. The injury may require medical assessment.
Do not plug the ear canal: cover the ear lightly and call emergency services. Blood or fluid from the ear after a head injury can signal serious injury.
The recovery position helps keep the airway clear and lets fluids drain from the mouth, reducing the risk of choking.
A head injury can conceal damage that is not immediately apparent. After an accident or if there are danger signs, call emergency services even if the person downplays the problem.

If the person is breathing normally, the recovery position helps keep the airway clear; call emergency services and monitor breathing. If you suspect a spinal injury, avoid moving them and follow the responders' instructions.
For an unconscious person breathing normally, the recovery position helps keep the airway clear. If you suspect a spinal injury, avoid moving them and follow the responders' instructions.
The recovery position keeps the airway clear and lets fluids drain from the mouth; it does not speed up the heart.
Do not automatically raise the legs after a head injury: there may be other injuries. Call emergency services and avoid unnecessary movement, especially if you suspect a spinal injury.
In shock, the circulation does not deliver enough blood and oxygen to vital organs, including the brain and heart. It is an emergency.

For shock, a conscious person may be laid on their back with legs raised to help circulation if they have no head, neck, back or leg injury. Call emergency services immediately; do not raise the legs if this causes pain or harm.
Severe bleeding reduces circulating blood and can prevent organs from receiving enough, causing shock. Emergency help is needed.
Confusion can occur in shock because circulation does not supply organs with enough oxygen. It is a sign to take seriously.
In shock the pulse may be rapid and weak as the body responds to inadequate circulation. Call emergency services immediately.
A markedly flushed face is not a typical sign of shock: skin may instead be pale, cold and sweaty. Symptoms can vary.
Blood pressure can fall in shock when circulation fails to supply the organs adequately. If you suspect shock, do not wait for a measurement before calling emergency services.
A superficial graze alone does not indicate shock. Shock involves inadequate circulation and can follow severe blood loss.
Do not give alcohol or other drinks to a person in shock. Call emergency services and help them while waiting.
The recovery position is not a stimulant for shock: it helps keep the airway clear in an unconscious person who is breathing.
Continuous shouting alone does not identify shock. Possible signs include pallor, cold sweat, confusion and a rapid, weak pulse.
Pallor, cold sweaty skin and shivering can accompany shock when circulation is inadequate. Not all symptoms need be present.
Insecticides are not wound treatments. Stop the bleeding and use a clean dressing; clean small wounds once bleeding has stopped.
Do more than call for help: direct pressure on the wound also helps control venous bleeding. If severe, call emergency services and maintain pressure.

The quiz marks this TRUE, but does not say whether it means pressure on the wound or on an artery at a distant pressure point. Current guidance is to call emergency services and promptly apply firm direct pressure to the wound; for severe uncontrolled bleeding follow the dispatcher’s instructions. The usefulness of distant pressure points is uncertain.
The priority is to control bleeding and get help if it is severe: major blood loss can be life-threatening. The priority is not keeping the road clean.
Severe arterial bleeding can quickly be fatal. Call emergency services and apply direct pressure to the wound to control blood loss.
A wound can become infected. After stopping bleeding, clean small wounds and cover them with a clean dressing; serious wounds need medical attention.
Severe arterial bleeding can quickly cause fatal shock. Apply pressure to the wound immediately and call emergency services.
Do not remain inactive: apply pressure to the wound with clean material and call emergency services immediately if bleeding is severe.
Intoxication does not remove the need for help: control the bleeding with pressure on the wound and protect yourself from contact with blood.
A plaster will not necessarily control severe arterial bleeding. Apply firm pressure to the wound and call emergency services immediately.
Severe blood loss can quickly cause shock. Apply pressure to the wound immediately and call emergency services.

The quiz marks this TRUE, but not every belt or tie is suitable. For life-threatening limb bleeding, a commercial tourniquet is preferred; if unavailable, only in an emergency can broad cloth be used for a correctly constructed improvised tourniquet. A leather belt may not work: call emergency services and follow their instructions.
Gloves or another waterproof barrier reduce contact with blood and the risk of transmitting infection while providing aid.
Do not enlarge a bleeding wound: instead try to control bleeding with pressure and clean material.
The danger inherent in severe venous bleeding is blood loss and possible shock, not choking. Any airway problems still need separate assessment.
Direct pressure with a sterile dressing, if available, helps reduce blood loss from the wound.
Anaesthesia does not stop bleeding. First apply pressure to the wound and seek emergency help if bleeding is severe.
A clean, preferably sterile dressing helps protect the wound while pressure is applied to control bleeding.
Venous blood generally flows steadily; pulsating spurts are typical of arterial bleeding. Either can be serious.

The quiz marks this FALSE: direct pressure is needed to control a bleeding wound; cold is not a reliable substitute. This does not mean cold can never affect blood vessels. If bleeding is severe, call emergency services immediately.
Heavy blood loss can quickly cause shock. Call emergency services immediately and apply pressure to the wound.

The quiz marks this FALSE: arterial blood may spurt with the heartbeat, unlike the generally steadier flow from a vein. “Continuous” is ambiguous: arterial blood does not have to stop between beats. Treat severe bleeding immediately without waiting to identify the vessel.
An arterial injury can cause rapid, extensive blood loss and fatal shock; control the bleeding immediately and call emergency services.
Venous blood generally flows without the pulsating spurts typical of arterial blood. Heavy venous bleeding remains an emergency.
After bleeding has stopped, a small dirty wound can be rinsed with clean water to remove dirt; seek medical assessment if it remains dirty.
Arterial blood can emerge in pulsating jets synchronized with the heartbeat. Such bleeding requires immediate control and urgent help.
A broken rib can cause chest pain, particularly when the chest moves during inhalation or coughing.

Call emergency services. The absence of a known back injury does not itself require moving the person: avoid unnecessary movement, but move them if necessary for safety, CPR or control of life-threatening bleeding. Follow the dispatcher’s instructions.

A conscious person with a chest injury may find a semi-seated position more comfortable; do not force it. If a head, neck or back injury is suspected, avoid moving them unless necessary for safety or lifesaving care, and follow emergency instructions.
If the person is unresponsive and not breathing normally, call emergency services and begin CPR: a suspected fracture does not justify inaction.
While waiting for emergency services, avoid unnecessary movement after trauma, keep the person comfortable and monitor breathing.

The quiz marks this FALSE: making someone cough or speak is not a general rule after an accident. A suspected rib fracture after a serious accident needs urgent assessment; during recovery, breathing normally and coughing when needed helps clear the lungs. The question does not distinguish these stages.

The recovery position helps keep the airway open for an unresponsive person breathing normally; a rib fracture alone does not automatically require it. Assess breathing and condition and call for help.
After cooling the burn, cover it loosely with a sterile, non-fluffy dressing if available to protect it from contamination.
Do not pull off stuck fabric: this can further damage the skin. Remove only clothing that is not attached to the burn.
Do not indiscriminately undress the person: leave clothing stuck to burned skin in place and carefully remove only clothing that is not stuck.
A blanket can smother flames on clothing by cutting off air. Intervene only if it is safe to do so.
Calling emergency services matters, but it does not mean withholding all help: provide first aid if the scene is safe. Do not enter a dangerous area.
Cool running water cools the burned area and limits heat damage; avoid ice and excessively cold water.
Do not remove stuck fabric: pulling it off can worsen the injury. Leave anything attached to the skin in place.
Hot water does not cool the injury. Use cool running water, not ice, to reduce heat damage.
A closed fracture also needs care: keep the limb still in the position found and seek help, avoiding unnecessary movement or attempts to straighten it.
A fracture is a break in a bone. It is nondisplaced when the fragments remain aligned and displaced when they have moved from their normal position.
A fracture does not prevent covering the person to keep them warm; avoid moving the injured part while helping.
A fracture is a broken bone, not internal bleeding. However, bleeding and other injuries can accompany a fracture.

A limb can be supported and immobilized with improvised materials without straightening it, but only if you know how to do so without increasing pain. If help will arrive soon, keep it still in the position found.
A closed fracture also needs medical assessment: intact skin does not rule out a broken bone or other complications.
Do not give alcohol or other drinks: the person may need anesthesia. Keep the limb still and seek help.
Taking the temperature immediately is not the priority for a suspected fracture. Assess the person, keep the injured part still and seek help.
An open fracture has a wound to protect with a sterile or clean dressing; in a closed fracture the skin is intact and there is no wound over the fracture to cover.

The quiz marks this FALSE: support depends on the site and circumstances. Keep a suspected injured limb still and supported without straightening it; ribs are not splinted like a limb, and breathing must be preserved. Follow emergency-service instructions.
Keeping the limb still in the position found limits movement at the fracture and the risk of worsening the injury. Do not try to straighten it.
If you suspect a spinal injury, keep the injured person still and call for help: unnecessary movement can worsen the injury. Follow rescuers’ instructions and act if necessary to save life.
If nobody is injured, an ambulance is not automatically necessary. Stop, make traffic safe and exchange useful information; call medical help if needed.
The owner’s operation and maintenance manual is not among the traffic documents listed in article 180. After an accident, provide affected people with identification and useful information.
The insurance certificate is among the documents to carry while driving and contains information useful for compensation. After an accident, provide useful information to affected people.
If the vehicles cannot be removed, the traffic police can be called to help manage the obstruction and safety.
Drivers must provide injured or damaged parties with their personal details and other useful information; they need not wait for the police.
Anyone involved must stop and give any injured people the necessary assistance; immediately leaving to go to the Carabinieri does not fulfill these duties.
The driving licence identifies the driver and supplies their details; it must be carried when driving.
The warning triangle is not prohibited by day: outside built-up areas it is required even by day when a stopped vehicle cannot be seen from a sufficient distance, in the cases specified.
There is no general prohibition on getting out before the police arrive. You may need to get out to warn of danger, wearing a reflective vest when required.
When only property is damaged, those involved must, where possible, avoid obstructing traffic while protecting safety.
Spreading a slippery substance would extend the area where vehicles can lose grip. Instead, prevent further danger and warn of the obstruction.
Staying calm helps you assess the situation and take the necessary steps for assistance and safety without acting hastily.

The quiz marks this FALSE, but not all legal costs are excluded: the statement does not specify which costs or who incurs them. Article 1917 of the Civil Code places the costs of defending the insured against the injured party’s action on the insurer, subject to statutory limits and conditions.
Drivers can fill in the form themselves, even separately if they disagree about what happened; an officer need not be present.
When only property is damaged, obstruction must be avoided where possible: do not leave a vehicle blocking traffic while filling in the form first.
The triangle gives approaching drivers advance warning of a stopped vehicle or obstruction in the cases specified.
You do not have to stay in the vehicle until the tow truck arrives: you may need to get out to warn of the danger, taking the required precautions and wearing the prescribed vest.
If the vehicle cannot be moved, roadside assistance can be called to remove it while the obstruction is marked in the meantime.
The CAI form is useful for reporting the accident, but it is not essential to request direct compensation.
The triangle is placed behind the obstruction so that drivers approaching from behind can see it and react in time.
The certificate of ownership is not among the documents required for driving. Depending on the case, the vehicle uses the registration document or the unified document.
The triangle warns approaching drivers of the obstruction so they can slow down and approach the danger area cautiously.
If the vehicle cannot be removed immediately, prevent it from becoming a danger: stay to manage the situation and warn of the obstruction, asking for help if needed.
The registration document records the person in whose name the vehicle is registered and provides their details; it is among the documents to carry when driving.
The form records the accident details and circumstances: complete it with the available information and sign knowingly, rather than signing it blank.
When only property is damaged, calling the police is not always mandatory: drivers must still exchange details and, where possible, avoid obstructing traffic.
A crest does not prohibit advance warning: if it limits visibility of the obstruction, the warning triangle must be placed where approaching road users can see it.
The licence identifies the driver and the registration document records the person in whose name the vehicle is registered; both help collect information after the accident.
A stopped vehicle can be an unexpected obstacle: warn approaching traffic and make the road safe.
118 is for medical emergencies. If there is only property damage and nobody needs medical help, an ambulance is not required.
The warning helps approaching drivers notice the obstacle in time and adjust their driving.
A car radio does not warn other road users of danger. Use a suitable warning, such as the triangle where required.
Slippery substances can make the road dangerous: whoever could not prevent the spill must warn traffic and notify the road authority or police.
Recording visible damage helps document the consequences for a compensation claim, while first safeguarding traffic safety.
A warning alerts approaching traffic to danger or an obstacle so drivers can respond; it does not necessarily prohibit passage through roadworks.
With only property damage, calling the Carabinieri is not always compulsory: stop, make the scene safe and give affected parties the relevant details.

When only property is damaged, clearing the road when possible reduces danger and obstruction; the damage can then be assessed. Protect traffic safety and, where compatible, preserve useful evidence; assist any injured people.
When only property is damaged, drivers must avoid obstructing traffic; moving vehicles when possible reduces the risk to others.

The absence of injuries does not make the warning triangle useless. Outside built-up areas, a vehicle stopped on the carriageway, excluding bicycles, two-wheeled mopeds and motorcycles, must be marked when it cannot be seen from behind at a sufficient distance, or at night if its rear position or hazard lights are missing or ineffective.
Recording circumstances, vehicle positions and witnesses helps reconstruct the accident and assess responsibility, while keeping safety in mind.
Drivers must give affected parties their personal details and other information useful for compensation, communicating by available means if they are absent.
Driving without RCA cover is punishable; the owner may be jointly liable under the conditions laid down by law.
If the responsible person directly and fully compensates the damage, they fulfil their obligation to the affected party. RCA is a separate means of covering liability.
RCA covers liability for damage to third parties arising from vehicle use. Affected parties can include people outside the vehicle, subject to applicable limits and exclusions.
An investment adviser is not required to handle an accident. Instead, exchange relevant details and follow the appropriate compensation procedures.
Property damage alone can give rise to civil liability to the affected party: the absence of injuries does not remove the duty to compensate.
Compensation can also be settled through the insurer’s procedure without waiting for a final court judgment.
A person who causes property damage may have to compensate it: civil liability also covers damage to property.

RCA covers liability for harm to third parties arising from vehicle use, not theft of the cargo as such. If goods are entrusted to a carrier, any liability the carrier has for their loss is separate and may be covered by specific insurance, subject to the policy terms.
RCA also covers property damage caused to third parties by vehicle use, subject to the cover’s limits and exclusions.
Routine maintenance is a vehicle operating expense, not damage to a third party caused by vehicle use and covered by RCA.
A driver who caused only property damage can also consult a road-accident technical expert, who can help assess the damage and circumstances and deal with the claim.
The fact that damage is only material does not exclude liability toward a passenger: their property can also be damaged, subject to any insurance exclusions.
Mandatory motor liability insurance covers liability to third parties for property damage caused by vehicle use, within the policy limits.
Driving without the required insurance carries an administrative fine and the vehicle is impounded.
Liability insurance covers damage that the insured is liable to compensate to a third party.
Damage to a pedestrian’s property can also make the driver liable: the absence of injury does not eliminate the right to compensation.
Basic motor liability insurance covers liability to third parties, not vandalism damage to one’s own vehicle; that requires separate cover.
Theft of one’s own vehicle is not covered by basic motor liability insurance: a separate guarantee is needed for that risk.
The policy is the contract under which the insurer assumes the insured risk and the policyholder pays the premium; the insured is the person protected by the cover.
Under direct compensation, when its conditions are met, the injured party requests compensation from their own insurer, which handles the claim.
Proof of vehicle tax payment is not required to report the accident: the useful details identify the vehicles, people, insurers and circumstances.
Direct action allows the injured party to claim from the liable party’s insurer, within the coverage limits.
A passenger who saw the accident may describe in writing what they observed; whether testimony is admissible in court also depends on their interest in the case.
The form asks for identifying details of witnesses, not the tax code of everyone involved or present.
Drivers’ signatures do not need authentication by officers; joint signature creates the statutory presumption about the stated circumstances.
The form asks for vehicle and insurance details, not the Community transport licence.

A satellite device can supply accident data, but its presence alone does not decide how to report a claim. IVASS considers the accident report form useful, although it says the form is not necessary to report a claim for direct compensation.
The form has space for witnesses’ names, addresses and contact details, which help establish what happened.
The form distinguishes the policyholder or insured from the driver: the driver’s details are entered even when that is a different person.

Licence details help identify the driver and handle the claim. The quiz says to record the number, issue date and place; the current IVASS form instead asks for the number, category and expiry date, not the place of issue. Copy the document accurately and give affected people the useful information.
Direct compensation concerns accidents involving identified and insured vehicles; registration and insurance alone are not enough, as other conditions also apply.
The form asks for the driver’s licence details, not the professional driver qualification card details.
The policy number goes in the insurance section to identify each vehicle’s cover.
To identify vehicles, record the registration plate or chassis number and country of registration; the form does not ask for the first registration date.
The insurer’s name goes in each vehicle’s insurance section along with the other policy details.
Direct compensation can apply to a collision between two vehicles if the other conditions are also met.
The form identifies the drivers and their licences, but does not require health card numbers.
The insurer and policy details identify the other party’s cover and help report the accident and seek compensation.
The drivers complete the form; their joint signatures record their agreed account. A municipal police signature is not required.

The quiz marks this TRUE: record the driver’s and owner’s details, the registration plate and the insurer; if a Green Card is shown, record its number too. These details help identify the insurer and handle the claim. Not every vehicle registered outside the EU necessarily has to show a Green Card.
The form covers people, vehicles, insurance and the circumstances of the accident; it does not require tachograph card details.
The absence of motorcycles alone is not enough: direct compensation requires other conditions, including two identified and insured vehicles. A motorcycle can also qualify.
Recording licence, vehicle and insurance details identifies the driver, vehicle and cover for the accident report.
The insured parties’ names identify the parties to the respective cover and belong on the form.
The form reports the accident to your insurer. If both drivers sign, the agreed account carries a rebuttable presumption about the circumstances; if they disagree, each can complete it separately.
Mileage is not required for the report: identifying details of the parties, vehicles and insurers and the accident circumstances are needed instead.
The absence of buses alone does not trigger direct compensation: conditions concerning the vehicles, insurance and accident must also be met.
The circumstances and diagram help reconstruct the accident and assess responsibility.
Breaking a safety rule does not automatically exclude an occupational accident: a worker’s fault can still be compatible with cover if the work connection exists.
INAIL covers occupational accidents under compulsory insurance law; it does not compensate all damage covered by the private insurance code.
Loading and unloading are connected with the driver’s work: an injury caused by a sudden event during them can be an occupational accident.
If the tyre is changed for work, a musculoskeletal injury caused by a sudden event during the operation can qualify as an occupational accident.
Climbing into the cab during work is connected with the job; a fall causing a fracture is a sudden event that can qualify as an occupational accident.
Coupling a trailer is connected with work: a hand injury caused by a sudden event during coupling can be an occupational accident.
A fall from the load platform during work is a sudden event connected with work; the resulting injury can be an occupational accident.
Being in the depot at the end of a shift does not itself exclude cover: an injury caused by a sudden event can be an occupational accident if connected with work.
A work connection does not require the vehicle to be moving: an injury during work with the vehicle stationary can also be an occupational accident.
During maintenance performed for work, an injury caused by a sudden event can be an occupational accident; the connection with the activity matters.
Driving on duty creates a work-related risk: an injury from a road accident can therefore be an occupational accident.
Damage to goods concerns property; an occupational accident concerns personal injury caused by an event connected with work.
Climbing onto and working on the load platform exposes the driver to an occupational risk of falling when the activity is work-related.
Handling a load can expose the driver to injury during an operation connected with the job, so it is an occupational risk.
The tourist is travelling as a passenger, not doing the driver’s work. An accident does not become a workplace accident merely because it occurs on the bus.
Negligence in using protective equipment does not automatically rule out a workplace accident. The connection with work matters, except in particular cases of voluntary risk unrelated to the work.
There must be a sudden injurious cause connected with work, producing an injury with disabling consequences. An event at the workplace alone is not enough.

The quiz marks this TRUE: work-related harm to the body or its function can be an occupational accident. The insurance definition also requires a violent cause and a connection with work; a slowly developing occupational disease is distinct.
If the fall into the tank occurs during work, it is a sudden event connected with work; the resulting injury can be a workplace accident.
Drinking too much during rest is not in itself a workplace accident: it is not an injury caused by a sudden event in connection with work.
Accidental contact with corrosive material during transport is a sudden event connected with work; the resulting eye injury can be a workplace accident.
A fire during transport operations can expose the driver to burns and other injuries.
Driving errors occur in many crashes: distraction, speed and failure to yield are examples. Road and vehicle factors can also contribute.
Excessive or inappropriate speed leaves less room to react and stop; excessive speed is among the most frequent circumstances recorded in crashes.
Failing to yield can cause paths to cross without the necessary clearance; it is among the most frequent circumstances recorded in crashes.
Distraction takes attention away from the road and can delay recognition of danger; it is among the most frequent circumstances recorded in crashes.
Following too closely can leave too little room to stop when the vehicle ahead slows down. Insufficient distance is a significant recorded crash circumstance.
Fatigue reduces alertness and can lengthen reaction times, increasing crash risk.
Defective suspension can impair control of the vehicle and contribute to a crash.
Worn tread provides less grip, especially on wet roads, increasing the risk of losing control.
If the brakes malfunction, stopping can become difficult or impossible, potentially causing a crash.
The tachograph records journey data and driver activity; its failure is not among the most frequent crash causes. Common circumstances include distraction, failure to yield and speed.
An injection pump failure is not among the most frequent recorded crash causes; common errors include distraction, failure to yield and excessive speed.
An extinguisher is used to tackle a fire in its early stages. Its absence concerns fire response and is not a direct cause of a road collision.

The quiz marks this FALSE, but that does not mean there is no risk: the pump circulates coolant, and a failure can cause overheating and engine stalling. In some cases loss of propulsion can increase crash risk.

The quiz marks this FALSE. A clogged air filter restricts engine air and can cause irregular operation: check and replace it according to the manufacturer’s instructions. The question specifies neither the severity of the fault nor evidence that every blockage increases crash risk.
The quiz marks this FALSE: fuel type alone does not automatically increase crash risk. Vehicle condition and driving also matter, and fuel systems require safety measures appropriate to the fuel.
Traffic psychology studies how personal and social factors influence travel and driving choices, including to promote safety and sustainable mobility.
Concentration helps a driver observe traffic and recognize hazards. If attention moves elsewhere, driving decisions and reactions can deteriorate.
Attention is essential: it lets drivers notice traffic information and react to hazards. When attention is diverted, driving performance deteriorates.
Mental demands change with the situation: in heavy traffic or poor visibility, detecting and tracking hazards can require more attention.
Mental demands are not independent of the environment: heavy traffic and poor visibility can make detecting and tracking hazards more demanding.
Experience can make driving situations more familiar and reduce some forms of anxiety. It does not automatically guarantee composure or freedom from risk.
Anger and frustration can encourage aggressive reactions and risky or rule-breaking behavior; other people’s behavior can also affect a driver’s emotional state.
Tension and fatigue can impair attention and reactions. Recognizing them and stopping to rest when necessary helps manage them.
Heavy traffic and critical situations can cause stress and affect a driver’s emotions and reactions: it is untrue that this can never happen.
The norms and habits of the social environment can influence attitudes toward risk and therefore driving behavior.
Habits, attitudes and experiences, including those formed in the family and social environment, can influence how drivers assess risks and react.

The quiz marks this TRUE. Unrealistic optimism and an illusion of control can distort judgments of one’s abilities and hazards. Actual risk and perceived risk are distinct concepts, not biases in themselves; distorted judgments can make them differ.
Unrealistic optimism can lead drivers to underestimate risk or overestimate their control over a situation, distorting their judgment.
The 95% figure is an estimate of crashes in which a human factor contributes, not a share attributable exclusively to people: vehicles and roads can also contribute.
A technical cause can also have a human component: for example, low pressure due to missed checks can contribute to tire failure.
Managing emotions helps maintain attention and avoid impulsive reactions that can compromise driving.
Reacting promptly to a hazard leaves more room to take action. Fatigue and distraction can slow the response.
Watching surrounding traffic is essential to detect hazards and decide how to respond, so the ability to monitor the situation matters.
Sensorimotor coordination turns what a driver perceives into actions on the controls, such as steering or braking; it is not useless.
Looking for or adjusting radio or navigation controls can take eyes, hands and attention away from driving, with potentially serious consequences.
Lighting a cigarette or looking for the ashtray can divert eyes, hands and attention from driving and increase crash risk.

The quiz marks this FALSE, but “looking at oneself in the mirror” is ambiguous. Checking traffic in the mirror is part of safe driving; looking at oneself for grooming can distract. The wording does not establish which use is meant.
The situation changes continually: drivers need to distribute attention and shift their gaze between the road, vehicles and other road users to detect hazards in time.
Personal protective equipment, selected for the risks of the work, protects its wearer during activities involving those risks.
Gloves exist to protect hands from mechanical, chemical or electrical hazards. They must be chosen for the specific hazard: no single type protects against everything.
Suitable safety glasses, masks and face shields can protect eyes from particles and corrosive splashes. The choice depends on the hazard and coverage needed.
The employer takes part in safety management: they assess risks when choosing protective equipment and provide suitable equipment to workers.
The supervisor oversees the work and checks that workers follow safety rules.
The workers’ safety representative participates in prevention: they are consulted on risk assessment and may make observations and proposals.
A production-site safety representative is provided for in certain settings with multiple companies or worksites and coordinates the representatives of the companies present.
The manager also implements the employer’s instructions, organizing and overseeing work for safety purposes.
The occupational physician contributes to risk assessment and carries out health surveillance where required.
Minimizing the number of workers exposed means that, if the hazard materializes, fewer people can suffer harm.
Protection includes health checks: health surveillance takes place where required, taking workplace risks into account.
Signs warn of hazards and communicate safety instructions; they supplement other preventive measures.
Reducing risk at source and replacing dangerous things with safer or non-dangerous alternatives are general protective measures: they reduce the hazard or workers’ exposure before harm occurs.
Limiting the use of chemical, physical and biological agents in the workplace is a general protective measure: using them less can reduce workers’ opportunities for exposure and therefore the risk.
Risk concerns the probability that a hazard will cause harm under the conditions of use or exposure; a hazard is the property capable of causing harm.
Assessment considers both the probability of an event and the possible severity of harm when choosing preventive measures.

Comparing serious and fatal accidents over time and analysing their circumstances helps identify recurring risks and guide prevention. These cases are especially important because they reveal very serious consequences, including loss of life.
The probability that a hazard will cause harm is a component of risk and must be considered in assessment, alongside possible severity.
The employer must ensure workers receive information and education and, where required, practical training for their duties.
An occupational injury is linked to work and to a violent cause; it can occur outside the usual workplace if connected with work and resulting in injury.
INAIL covers occupational injuries of insured people when the required conditions are met; recognition requires assessment of the case.
A violent cause is a rapid, concentrated action that produces an injury; it differs from the prolonged exposure typical of many occupational diseases.
The connection with work links the event to the conditions in which work is performed, including when work indirectly creates the risky situation.
An occupational injury has a harmful consequence, such as temporary incapacity or permanent impairment; death may also result.
A violent cause is an element of an occupational injury: it means a rapid, concentrated injurious action, not necessarily an assault.
Slipping while climbing into a cab at work is a sudden event connected with transport work: a resulting injury can constitute an occupational injury.
Coupling or uncoupling a trailer is a work operation: a sudden injury during it can constitute an occupational injury.
A fall from a loading platform during work can cause an occupational injury: the fall is a sudden event connected with transport work.
Accidental contact with corrosive cargo during work can cause injury through a violent cause and constitute an occupational injury.
Crashes during transport can injure workers and other road users, so road risk must be considered.
Fatigue reduces attention and speed of reaction, increasing the chance of errors and crashes.
Road crash risk cannot be excluded: a collision during transport can cause injuries.
Alcohol impairs driving and increases crash risk, even at low concentrations.
Using a phone distracts from driving and can slow reactions to hazards, increasing crash risk.
Alcohol is a risk factor: it impairs driving and increases the chance of a crash.
Even occasional use can lead to driving under the influence: the effects on driving increase crash risk.
The assessment must cover all health and safety risks, including those from occasional handling of dangerous goods.
Occasional handling does not remove the obligation: when residual risks cannot be sufficiently controlled by other means, suitable PPE must be selected based on the assessment.
Climbing onto the vehicle for loading or unloading exposes workers to risks such as falls; the employer must assess them and establish preventive measures.
Accessing the top of a tank vehicle can also cause a fall; the body type does not remove the duty to assess risks.
Protective retroreflective clothing is PPE: it makes a person exposed to traffic more visible.
The rules govern driving, breaks and rest to improve working conditions and road safety, not to reduce vehicle wear.
Driving 100 km is not required: a person is a driver even when driving briefly or travelling on board to drive if necessary.
Limiting driving and providing breaks and rest protects working conditions and safety by addressing fatigue risks.
The rules aim to improve working conditions and road safety, not reduce vehicle emissions.
The rules aim to improve working conditions and road safety, not contain wages.
Driving, break and rest rules aim to improve drivers’ working conditions and road safety.
A person carried on board as part of their duties to drive if necessary is also a driver.
The definition includes a person who drives even briefly; no minimum distance is required.
The definition also includes a person carried on board as part of their duties to drive if necessary.
Breaks and rest limit fatigue-related risk; improved road safety also protects other road users.
The tachograph distinguishes driving, other work, availability and breaks or rest; the driver selects activities and enters the required periods.

The regulation covers goods transport where maximum permissible mass, including any trailer, exceeds 3.5 tonnes, subject to exceptions. Since 1 July 2026 it also covers some international or cabotage operations over 2.5 tonnes.
The rules cover passenger transport in vehicles constructed or adapted for more than nine people including the driver, subject to exceptions.

The regulation applies to transport within the EU by buses designed for more than nine people, including the driver, and to goods transport with a total mass exceeding 3.5 t, subject to the specified exceptions.

The regulation applies to transport between the EU and European Economic Area states for the categories indicated, subject to the specified exceptions; for buses, the relevant capacity is more than nine people, including the driver.

The FALSO verdict rules out a general obligation: from 1 July 2026, the regulation also covers vehicles over 2.5 t in international transport or cabotage, subject to exceptions. The mass includes any trailers.
It is incorrect to apply the AETR to a journey entirely between Italy and France: Regulation EC 561/2006 applies to transport within the EU, subject to its exceptions.
For transport entirely within the EU, the regulation applies regardless of the country of registration, provided the transport falls within its scope.
The 80 km threshold is incorrect: the exclusion applies to regular services with a route not exceeding 50 km.
The regulation excludes vehicles used in emergencies or rescue operations, including those used for the non-commercial transport of humanitarian aid.
Regular services with a route not exceeding 50 km are excluded from Regulation EC 561/2006.
A speed of 50 km/h does not trigger this exclusion: it applies to vehicles whose maximum authorised speed does not exceed 40 km/h.
The regulation excludes vehicles or vehicle combinations up to 7.5 t used for the non-commercial transport of goods.
Vehicles with a maximum authorised speed not exceeding 40 km/h are excluded from the regulation.
A trailer does not create an exemption: in goods transport, the mass of the trailer is considered together with that of the vehicle, subject to the other exceptions provided for.
Hiring a vehicle with a driver is not in itself an exemption: the regulation covers passenger transport in vehicles suitable for more than nine people, including the driver, subject to exceptions.
Use by a sports club does not automatically result in an exemption: the type of transport and any applicable exceptions must be assessed.
Vehicles undergoing road tests for repair or maintenance are excluded.

It is not true that mass is irrelevant: for goods, the usual threshold is over 3.5 t, including trailers; from 1 July 2026 it is over 2.5 t for international transport or cabotage, subject to exceptions.
Periodic inspection of the tachograph does not exempt a driver from driving limits: their application depends on the transport and the exclusions in the regulation.
Fire service vehicles are excluded when the transport takes place within the scope of the service’s duties and under its control.
It does not apply to every service: for example, regular services with a route not exceeding 50 km are excluded.
Specialised vehicles used to remove broken-down vehicles are excluded when operating within 100 km of their operating base.
Travelling on a motorway is not enough for an exemption: for roadside assistance, the rule requires specialised vehicles operating within 100 km of their operating base.
Armed forces vehicles are excluded if the transport falls within the duties assigned to the service and takes place under its control.
The presence of a second driver does not allow the first to drive for more than 4 and a half hours without a break: each driver must take the required break.
The 4 and a half hours refer to the driving period before a break, not the daily maximum. The daily limit is 9 hours, extendable to 10 no more than twice a week.
After 4 and a half hours of driving, the driver must take a break of at least 45 minutes, which may be split as provided by the rules, unless they begin a rest period.
Fitness does not replace a break. Within 4½ hours of driving, take a break of at least 45 minutes or a rest period; the break may be split into at least 15 minutes followed by at least 30.

Subject to the exemptions, the regulation covers transport between the EU and Switzerland in goods vehicles whose maximum permissible mass, including any trailer or semi-trailer, exceeds 3.5 tonnes, and in vehicles constructed or permanently adapted and intended to carry more than nine people including the driver. Since 1 July 2026 it also covers international goods transport where the maximum permissible mass, including any trailer or semi-trailer, exceeds 2.5 tonnes.
The normal daily driving limit is 9 hours; it may be extended to 10 hours no more than twice a week, not three times.
Daily driving time totals driving between two daily rests, or between a daily and a weekly rest; it does not necessarily match a calendar day.
The normal daily driving limit is 9 hours; it can rise to 10 hours at most twice a week.
The 9 hours are the normal total daily limit, not a continuous stretch: after 4½ hours of driving a break or rest is required.
The normal daily limit is 9 hours, extendable to 10 no more than twice a week; 8 hours is not the prescribed maximum.
The total limit over two consecutive weeks is 90 hours, not 112; the 56-hour limit also applies to each week.
The weekly driving limit is 56 hours, not 45; the total over two consecutive weeks must not exceed 90 hours.
Total driving in two consecutive weeks must not exceed 90 hours; the 56-hour limit also applies to each week.
Weekly driving must not exceed 56 hours; the 90-hour limit for two consecutive weeks and working-time limits also apply.
The break is solely for rest: during it, the driver may neither drive nor perform other duties.
The threshold is 4½ hours of driving, not 4. A full break may also be taken earlier; within 4½ hours take at least 45 minutes, possibly split, or a rest period.
The break is not optional: within 4½ hours of driving take a break of at least 45 minutes or a rest period. The break may be split into at least 15 minutes followed by at least 30.
The 45-minute break may be replaced by at least 15 minutes followed by at least 30 minutes, distributed over the driving period in that order.
A break is solely for recuperation: the driver neither drives nor performs other work during it.
Maintenance is work, so it cannot be done during a break, which is solely for recuperation.
Other work cannot be performed during a break: the break is solely for recuperation.
Within 4½ hours of driving take a break of at least 45 minutes or a rest period. The break may be split into at least 15 minutes followed by at least 30.
A break does not permit other work: it is a period without driving or other work, solely for recuperation.
Rest is an uninterrupted period during which the driver may freely dispose of their time; doing other work is not rest.

Being on call does not become rest because it is spent at home. For example, waiting for a call to start or resume driving or perform other work can be availability; rest requires freedom to dispose of one’s time.
Rest requires an uninterrupted period in which the driver may freely dispose of their time, without work or availability obligations.
Availability can include, for example, waiting for a call to start or resume driving or perform other work. It is not rest, which requires freedom to dispose of one’s time.

Regular daily rest is at least 11 hours, or it may be split into at least 3 hours followed by at least 9 hours. Reduced daily rest lasts at least 9 but less than 11 hours; at most three reductions are allowed between two weekly rest periods.
A reduced daily rest period lasts at least 9 consecutive hours and less than 11; a period of 11 consecutive hours or more is a regular daily rest period.
Six consecutive hours are not enough: a reduced daily rest period must last at least 9 hours and less than 11.
A regular daily rest period requires at least 11 consecutive hours; the regulation also provides for split regular rest and, under certain conditions, reduced rest.
Eleven consecutive hours meet the minimum for a regular daily rest period; this can also be split under the specified conditions.
Normally, a new daily rest period must be taken within 24 hours of the end of the previous daily or weekly rest period. Exceptions are provided for, for example in multi-manning.
Seven consecutive hours do not meet the 11-hour minimum for a continuous regular daily rest period.
Regular rest can be split: first at least 3 consecutive hours, then at least 9 consecutive hours, in that order.
Daily rest may be taken in a stationary vehicle if it provides suitable sleeping accommodation.
A ferry is not the only case: daily rest may also be taken in a stationary vehicle with suitable sleeping accommodation.

An agreement with the employer does not allow the weekly rest requirement to be ignored: as a rule, it must begin within six 24-hour periods of the previous one. Specific exceptions exist, but they are not based on a simple agreement.
A reduced weekly rest period is less than 45 hours but must last at least 24 consecutive hours; the reduction is subject to conditions and compensation.
Twenty-four hours can constitute a reduced weekly rest period, but the minimum for a regular weekly rest period is 45 hours.

The quiz treats the general rule as true: weekly rest begins within six 24-hour periods of the previous one. However, this is not an absolute ban on driving on more than six calendar days: specific exceptions are also provided for.
A regular weekly rest period lasts at least 45 hours; a shorter rest period may be reduced only under the specified conditions.

To reach a suitable stopping place, the driving limit may be departed from only to the extent necessary to ensure safety, without compromising road safety. The reason must be recorded no later than on arrival.

For international transport subject to the rules that leaves the EU, Switzerland and the EEA, the AETR applies to the entire journey of a vehicle registered in the EU, including the journey to Russia.

For international transport subject to the rules that takes place partly outside the EU, Switzerland and the EEA, the AETR applies; the part of the journey affected also depends on the vehicle’s registration.
For national regular service without a tachograph, the required documents include an extract from the service register and a copy of the service timetable, not a copy of the employment contract.
In national regular service without a tachograph, the driver carries an extract from the service register and a copy of the timetable, which allow the organisation of shifts to be checked.

For national regular service without a tachograph, the regulation requires an extract from the service register and a copy of the timetable; it does not require a tachograph card to record that service.
Installation and repair are reserved for authorised fitters, workshops or manufacturers; periodic inspections must also be carried out by authorised workshops.
Three years is too long: the periodic tachograph inspection must be carried out at least every two years and includes a check of its operation.
Mass alone is not enough to make a tachograph mandatory for all vehicles: the scope depends on the transport performed, and exclusions are provided for, for example for certain armed forces vehicles.
The tachograph must be inspected by an authorised workshop at least every two years; the inspection also checks that it works correctly.
The tachograph records data including speed; it is not the device that prevents the vehicle from exceeding a speed.
The company must provide sheets of an approved type that are suitable for the installed tachograph.
The transport company provides the driver with a sufficient number of personal, compatible sheets.
A photocopy cannot replace a compatible sheet of an approved type: suitable spare sheets must be available.
The sheets are supplied by the transport company, not the chamber of commerce.

The sheet is used during the daily working period and is normally removed at the end; it must not be used beyond the period for which it is intended. Returning the vehicle does not necessarily coincide with the end of work.
The driver records the registration number of the first vehicle and of every other vehicle assigned to them while using the sheet.
The tachograph displays and records speed; it is not the device that limits the vehicle's speed.
The sheet is not automatically used for 36 hours: it cannot cover a period longer than the one for which it is intended.
The sheet is personal: when drivers change, the records must relate to the driver who is driving.
The tachograph's approval number is not among the details required on the sheet; the name, registration number and odometer reading are recorded, among other details.
The tachograph card number is not among the details required on the analogue sheet; the name, registration number and odometer reading are recorded, among other details.
The date of the tachograph's last inspection is not among the details required on the sheet; the name, registration number and odometer reading are recorded, among other details.
At the start of the first recorded journey, the odometer reading is recorded to document the distance travelled.
The vehicle's registration number is recorded at the start of the first recorded journey, as are the registration numbers of any subsequent vehicles if the driver changes vehicles.
At the start of using the sheet, the driver writes their first and last name on it to identify its holder.
The place where use of the sheet begins is recorded, as well as the place where it ends.
The date on which use of the sheet begins is recorded, and the end date is also recorded when use ends.
Filling in the sheet is not left entirely until the end: some details, such as the name and initial odometer reading, are entered at the beginning.
The driving licence and CQC numbers are not among the details required on the analogue sheet; the driver instead gives their first and last name.
The symbols distinguish the recorded activities: driving, other work, availability, and breaks or rest.
A mandatory break does not in itself require a new sheet: the sheet also records breaks and rest and must not be removed before the end of the working period unless authorised.
The tachograph automatically marks every opening of its casing on the sheet.
The selector is used to record separately the activity performed while the vehicle is stopped, such as other work, availability or rest.
If the sheet is compatible, changing vehicles does not require a new sheet: the registration numbers, odometer readings and time of the change are recorded.
Changing vehicles does not automatically require a new sheet: if compatible, the driver continues to use their personal sheet and records the details of the change.
The repair must be made as soon as circumstances permit. If the vehicle can return to base within a week, it may be repaired on its return.
The tachograph must be repaired as soon as possible by an authorised workshop. If returning to base takes more than a week from the breakdown, the repair must be made during the journey.
Manual records are required during the breakdown for periods that were not recorded correctly, even on short journeys; they do not depend on exceeding seven days.
A breakdown does not automatically require the journey to be stopped immediately: the device must be repaired as soon as possible and unrecorded periods must be recorded manually.

There is no requirement to stop immediately and communicate those details to the two recipients mentioned. During the breakdown, the driver records the unrecorded periods on the sheet or on a separate sheet, with identification and a signature.
During the breakdown, periods not recorded correctly must be recorded manually on the record sheet or on a separate sheet, with identifying details and a signature.
With an analogue tachograph, periods not recorded correctly because of a breakdown can be recorded on the back of the disc, adding identification and a signature; a separate sheet is also permitted.
Cleaning the vehicle is working time: since it is not driving, it is recorded as other work.
Loading and unloading are work activities other than driving and are recorded as other work.
Availability time has a separate category on the tachograph and is recorded separately from driving, other work and rest.
Checking tyre pressure is a technical check of the vehicle: it is work other than driving and is recorded as other work.
Work performed for another employer, inside or outside the transport sector, also counts as other work to be recorded.
Customs administrative formalities related to transport are work other than driving and must be recorded as other work.

A 50 km threshold does not apply: the driver must be able to produce the sheets required for the specified period. Since 31 December 2024, that period includes the current day and the preceding 56 days.

The sheets for the last 28 days fall within the period to be produced, but they are no longer sufficient: since 31 December 2024, the sheets for the current day and the preceding 56 days have been required.
A three-month period is not required for roadside presentation: since 31 December 2024, the driver must be able to produce the sheets for the current day and the preceding 56 days.
The memory records tachograph usage data, such as activity, distance and speed, not routine vehicle maintenance work.
When the card is removed at the end of the day, the vehicle must be stationary. The card must not be removed before the end of the daily working period unless authorised.
The card must be inserted before driving begins, while the vehicle is stationary. Inserting it while the vehicle is moving may be recorded as an event and is not the correct procedure.
The tachograph stores data about inserted and removed cards in its memory, including the times of those operations.
The memory also records the vehicle's speed; the detailed data include the instantaneous speed and the corresponding time.
The memory stores data about the last download of its contents to an external medium in company or calibration mode, including the date and time.
The fourth type is the control card, intended for inspection authorities; the chamber of commerce issues the cards but is not a type of card.
The card is used every day of driving from the moment the driver takes over the vehicle. It must not be removed before the end of the daily working period unless authorised.
In Italy, chambers of commerce issue tachograph cards, including the driver's personal card.
The driver card is personal: each driver uses their own, even within the same company.
The card identifies the driver and can only be used by its holder.
The card is used from taking over the vehicle until the end of the daily working period, unless its removal is authorized; it also records activities other than driving.
Each driver uses their own personal card, even when several people drive the same vehicle.
The four cards are intended for different users: drivers, companies, control authorities and workshops.
There is no need to wait 24 hours: the card remains inserted until the end of the daily working period, unless its removal is authorized.
The card is used from the time the driver takes over the vehicle to record their activities.
When there is more than one driver on board, each inserts their own card into the correct slot so that activities are attributed to the right person.
The second driver on board also inserts their own card into the correct slot: they do not wait until they start driving.
The tachograph records and displays data about the driver's activities and the vehicle; it does not warn of speed cameras on the road.
Speed is measured by the device; manual entries concern activities and their corresponding periods, not average speed.
The tachograph reports card-related events, such as a card inserted while driving or an invalid combination of cards.
A card-related error generates a warning: the tachograph records and alerts, but does not stop the vehicle.
The tachograph warns when the continuous driving limit is approaching and when it is reached, helping the driver comply with break requirements.
Losing the card does not mean the driver must stop immediately: they may continue temporarily under the prescribed conditions, requesting a replacement and documenting their activities.
The loss must be reported to the police, and the card must be blocked or replaced upon request.
Without a card, the driver must print the data at the beginning and end of the journey, add any unrecorded activities, identify themselves and sign; the printouts must be kept for inspections.

The quiz marks this as true, but the current rule refers to 15 calendar days, not working days. Driving may continue for longer only if necessary to return the vehicle to base and if it can be shown that the card could not be used.
A colleague's card cannot be used: it is personal. If a card is lost, the prescribed procedures for driving temporarily without one must be followed.

In the event of a breakdown, the driver records the periods that the tachograph does not record correctly, identifying themselves and signing. Note: the cited provision requires the times to be recorded, but does not specify a general obligation here to record the distance in kilometres.
For a broken tachograph, no temporary permit is requested from the Chamber of Commerce: the device is repaired and unrecorded periods are noted down.
‘Out of scope’ indicates use outside the scope of the applicable rules; it does not switch off the tachograph, but suspends certain warnings.
‘Out of scope’ indicates use outside the scope of the rules, not a malfunction. In the event of a breakdown, the device must be repaired and unrecorded periods entered manually.

The quiz indicates VERO: tampering with the tachograph is penalized. However, the wording is too general: Article 179 links licence suspension to driving with an altered device, not automatically to anyone who alters it.
When a tachograph is mandatory, driving with a device that does not work results in a fine and suspension of the driving licence.

Failure to insert the record sheet or card results in a loss of points. If the violation occurs during a service for which the CQC is required, the points are deducted from the professional qualification.
Tampering with the seals falls under the tachograph penalty: in addition to the prescribed fine, which is doubled, the driving licence is suspended even if the device itself has not been altered.
Driving with a non-functioning tachograph carries a fine and suspension of the driving licence, not confiscation of the vehicle.
When a tachograph is mandatory, driving without one results in an administrative fine and suspension of the driving licence, not arrest.
A tachograph with non-compliant specifications does not meet the requirement: the violation results in a fine and suspension of the driving licence.
If a tachograph is mandatory, driving without one can result in a fine and suspension of the driving licence.
Failing to insert the record sheet or card prevents correct recording: the violation carries a fine and suspension of the driving licence.

For altering a tachograph, the code provides for an administrative fine and suspension of the driving licence; it does not prescribe a court-imposed penalty solely because the offence is repeated twice within two years.
Tampering with the seals results in a doubled fine and suspension of the driving licence; revocation is not the penalty prescribed for this violation.
Tampering with the seals results in a doubled fine and suspension of the driving licence.

The holder of the licence or authorization who puts a vehicle with a tampered tachograph into service is subject to a fine. Suspension of the transport licence for repeated violations is separate from suspension of the driver's driving licence.
The holder of a transport licence or authorization who puts a vehicle into service without the required tachograph is subject to an administrative fine.

Professional transport of goods requires a licence appropriate to the vehicle and a CQC qualification, unless an exemption applies. The wording is general: above 3.5 tonnes, a C1 or C1E licence may also be sufficient within its respective limits.
Professional passenger transport by scheduled bus requires the passenger CQC qualification together with the appropriate driving licence: the CAP KB does not replace it.
Professional passenger transport by chartered bus with a driver requires the appropriate driving licence and the passenger CQC qualification.
The CQC is issued through a procedure handled by the Civil Motorization Office, not the Chamber of Commerce.
Professional passenger transport by scheduled bus requires the appropriate driving licence and the passenger CQC qualification.

The CQC supplements the driving licence for professional driving, but does not by itself authorize driving during a licence suspension. Any permit issued by the prefecture has its own conditions and limits.
Issuing the CQC is one of the procedures handled by the Civil Motorization offices.

A D or DE licence authorizes driving vehicles in the corresponding category, but does not by itself exempt the holder from the CQC requirement when carrying out professional transport subject to that requirement.
A professional scheduled bus driver must hold the passenger CQC qualification in addition to the appropriate driving licence.
Professional transport of passengers or goods in vehicles of the covered categories requires a CQC, including for employees of companies established in Italy, subject to the prescribed exemptions.
The requirement also applies to a professional driver from outside the EU employed by a company established in Italy, when driving vehicles in the covered categories and no exemption applies.
Transport of goods for private, non-commercial purposes is exempt from the CQC requirement. The MIT specifies that the exemption does not apply to someone hired as a driver.
Driving a school bus is not automatically exempt: the MIT requires a CQC for drivers of school buses for which a CAP KD was required.
The CQC starts with 20 points, separate from those on the driving licence; it does not start with 30 points.
The CQC qualification has its own balance of 20 points, separate from and additional to those on the Italian driving licence.
The CQC qualification lasts five years and is renewed through periodic training.
The CQC has its own five-year expiry date: it does not necessarily coincide with the driving licence expiry date, even though code 95 appears on the licence.
Work as a driver does not replace the periodic training required to renew the CQC.
Renewing the CQC requires attendance at a periodic training course.
Turning 60 does not automatically prevent renewal of the passenger transport CQC: the qualification requires periodic training, while the driving licence requirements must still be met.
Initial qualification is not the course required for renewal. After a prolonged period of expiry, the procedure depends on the applicable rules and may require a reinstatement or review exam.

For stays of up to three months, an identity document valid for travel abroad or a valid passport is sufficient. ‘Without restrictions’ should be understood as a general rule: the law provides for exceptions, for example on public policy grounds.

It is incorrect to require an EU citizen to have a residence card issued by the police headquarters for the first three months: an identity card valid for travel abroad or a valid passport is sufficient.
It is incorrect to demand a passport with a visa: an EU citizen can enter with an identity card valid for travel abroad or a valid passport, without an entry visa.

The quiz marks this as true, but a declaration of presence is not an exclusive condition for a stay: it is optional, and failure to make one creates a rebuttable presumption about the length of the stay. A passport is also valid.
To stay in another Member State for up to three months, an EU citizen must have a valid identity card or a valid passport.

The quiz marks this as true, referring to grounds of public policy, public security and public health. However, ‘only’ is too absolute: removal is also possible when the conditions for the right of residence are no longer met.
An EU citizen exercises the right of residence without a residence permit; beyond three months, however, they must meet the applicable conditions and apply for registration as a resident.
An EU citizen can travel between Member States with a valid identity card or passport, without an entry visa.
EU citizens have the right to free movement, but it can be restricted in cases provided for by law, for example on public policy or public security grounds.
The law allows restrictions on the entry of EU citizens on public policy grounds, subject to the applicable conditions and safeguards.
It is incorrect to require an EU citizen to have a visa: to enter and stay for up to three months, an identity document valid for travel abroad or a valid passport is sufficient.
Religion is not in itself grounds for removal. Restrictions may be imposed on grounds provided for by law, such as public policy, security or public health.

A valid passport and visa, when required, are entry documents; they are not sufficient on their own, however, because the other applicable conditions must also be met. Some non-EU citizens are exempt from the visa requirement for short stays.

At external borders, third-country nationals undergo entry checks; customs, currency and health checks may also apply. This is a general statement: it does not mean that every person always undergoes all these checks.
A visa is an authorisation issued to a foreign national to present themselves for entry, subject to the applicable conditions; it does not guarantee admission on its own.
A visa is not a signature placed on a stamp at the border: it is an entry authorisation issued by the competent authorities before travel, when required.
Not all EU countries belong to the Schengen area without internal border checks: Ireland is outside it, although it participates in some Schengen measures.
The Schengen area also includes non-EU countries, such as Switzerland and Norway: EU membership and participation in Schengen are separate matters.
As a rule, internal borders may be crossed at any point without border checks on persons. Police checks and temporarily reinstated border checks remain possible.
The rule is that there are no border checks on persons at internal borders; police checks and temporary reinstatement of border checks remain possible in specified cases.
The absence of internal checks goes hand in hand with common rules and checks on persons at the area's external borders.

In the event of a serious threat to public policy or internal security, a state may temporarily reinstate checks at internal borders, subject to specified conditions and limits; this does not suspend Schengen as a whole.
There are common rules for external borders and short-stay visas. Asylum is also governed by common European rules, with states participating in different areas.
It is checks at internal borders that are generally abolished; at external borders, people are subject to checks.
At internal borders, the rule is that there are no border checks on persons; strengthened checks concern external borders, although internal checks may be temporarily reinstated.
Schengen mainly concerns the movement of people and border checks; it does not grant goods vehicle drivers the tax relief described.
The absence of ordinary border checks does not eliminate the need for a valid travel document: it may be requested, for example, during police checks or when border checks are reinstated.
The principle allows internal borders to be crossed at any point without border checks on persons. Police checks and temporary reinstatement of border checks are still possible.
Poland belongs to both the EU and the Schengen area, so it participates in free movement across internal borders, subject to the specified exceptions.
Slovenia belongs to both the EU and the Schengen area, so it participates in free movement across internal borders, subject to the specified exceptions.
Latvia belongs to both the EU and the Schengen area, so it participates in free movement across internal borders, subject to the specified exceptions.
The United Kingdom left the EU on 31 January 2020 and has no longer been a Member State since then.
The agreement is a set of rules between states, not a personal document to be presented. The driver must, however, have the required travel documents and may be subject to applicable checks.
Serbia is a candidate for EU membership, not a Member State, and is not part of the Schengen area.
Ireland is an EU member but is not part of the Schengen area: it maintains its own visa and border control policy.
Ukraine is a candidate for EU membership and is not part of the Schengen area; being outside the EU is not enough to make a country part of Schengen.
Not all EU members are in the Schengen area: Ireland, for example, is outside it and maintains its own border controls.
Ireland belongs to the EU but not the Schengen area; it maintains its own visa and border control policy.
Entry and residence are subject to legal conditions: an irregular stay may lead to a return decision, subject to the applicable exceptions and safeguards, including the right to asylum.
The purpose of working does not make irregular entry lawful. For non-EU citizens to work as employees, authorisation and a visa are normally required before entry.

In general, there are no border checks on persons at internal Schengen borders, and goods in free circulation within the EU are not subject to customs checks at the border. Police checks and temporary reinstatement of checks on persons remain possible.

The quiz indicates VERO: border checks on persons are not normally carried out at internal Schengen borders, while Schengen does not in itself eliminate customs checks. The absence of identity checks is not absolute: police checks and temporary reinstatement of border checks are possible.
The free movement of goods within the EU customs area and the abolition of checks on people in the Schengen area are two different things: checks on people remain at the external Schengen border.

The quiz considers it true that customs checks and rules on goods and money apply at external borders. This is a general statement: actual obligations and checks depend on the border and the goods; for cash, a threshold may trigger a declaration requirement, not necessarily a ban on carrying it.
At external Schengen borders, people undergo border checks, including checks on their identity and documents; operational exceptions to ordinary checks are provided for.

Goods in free circulation between EU countries are not normally subject to customs checks at the border. Schengen, by contrast, concerns checks on people, which are normally absent at internal borders.
The customs union does not eliminate checks on people at an external Schengen border, so the claim that both types of checks are generally absent is incorrect.
The distinction is reversed: in the EU, goods in free circulation are not normally checked at internal customs borders, while people are checked at the external Schengen border.
Transporting goods across an external border is not generally prohibited: customs procedures, such as TIR transit, exist for movements involving non-EU countries.

Schengen governs checks on people, not the customs union: checks on people are normally absent at an internal Schengen border, but this does not automatically eliminate customs checks involving non-EU countries.
EU citizens enjoy freedom of movement and can enter with a valid passport or identity card; restrictions provided for by law remain possible, for example on public order grounds.
A valid travel document and passage through a border crossing are ordinary entry requirements at the external border; the other applicable conditions must also be met.
When a visa is required, it must be held in addition to meeting the other entry conditions: a visa alone does not guarantee admission.
A general exemption from checks is incorrect: checks on people are provided for at external borders, and customs and currency checks may apply depending on the circumstances.
Having relatives without criminal records does not replace entry formalities: documents and a visa are required when applicable, along with the other applicable conditions.
A visa does not give freedom to travel in every European country: its territorial validity and authorized duration depend on the visa and the rules of the countries concerned.
Not posing a threat to public order, security, public health or international relations is one of the conditions for entry for short stays, together with the other prescribed conditions.
For a short stay, sufficient means are required for the stay and return, or the ability to obtain them legally. A return ticket can also help demonstrate means for the journey.
An SIS alert for refusal of entry generally prevents entry for a short stay; the law provides for specific exceptions.
A passport and visa, when required, are essential documents, but they do not by themselves guarantee entry: the other applicable conditions must also be checked.
In addition to individual passports, Italian law provides for a collective passport for a group and a single journey, subject to the established conditions.
The Italian collective passport is intended for groups of 5 to 50 people and for a single journey: a group of at least one hundred people does not meet this limit.
An identity card valid for travel abroad is accepted in many countries, including EU countries, but it does not replace a passport at every border: the destination's requirements must be checked.
A visa is an authorization to enter, normally affixed as a sticker to a passport or other travel document; it does not automatically guarantee admission at the border.

The Italian diplomatic or consular mission responsible for the foreign national's place of residence normally has authority over the visa; in some cases another Schengen state may act as a representative.

The quiz indicates VERO, but an absolute ban on extensions is incorrect: an already issued visa can be extended, for example due to force majeure or humanitarian reasons, subject to the prescribed conditions.
The visa exemption for eligible nationalities applies to short stays, not stays exceeding 120 days: the ordinary Schengen limit is 90 days in any 180-day period.
The uniform Schengen visa for short stays allows a maximum of 90 days in any 180-day period, not 150.

Under the historical Schengen rules, a collective visa for transit or a stay had a duration of no more than 30 days, not 60. This is a historical provision, not a description of current visa categories.
An Italian visa is normally issued by the competent diplomatic or consular mission, not by a court.
A residence permit is not required for visits, business, tourism and study for up to three months; a declaration of presence is still required according to the applicable procedures.
