FALSO according to the quiz: the difficulties are explained not only by insufficient use of ships, but by an imbalance between modes. The wording is ambiguous because European policy also promotes transport by sea and inland waterways.
FALSO. In general, rail produces fewer greenhouse gas emissions per unit of goods transported than road transport; the comparison still depends on the service and the energy used.
VERO. In a general comparison, the accident rate for rail is lower than for road transport, although individual transport operations still carry risks.
VERO. Rail generally produces fewer greenhouse gas emissions per unit of freight transported than road transport, although the results depend on the service.
VERO. Rail generally offers a safety advantage: the accident rate in the rail sector is lower than in road transport.
VERO. Rail freight can reduce the climate impact of goods: it generally emits fewer greenhouse gases per unit transported than road transport.
FALSO. Rail follows a fixed network and does not reach every destination: road transport has wider coverage and can handle the first and last legs.

FALSO according to the quiz: rail does not always guarantee faster transport, because transfers and journeys to and from terminals can lengthen the trip. Actual speed depends on the route and service, however.
VERO. Rail depends on lines and terminals; reaching the sender and recipient directly often requires adding a road leg to the journey.
FALSO. Rail freight generally requires less energy per tonne-kilometre than trucks; the actual result depends on the service.
VERO. Rail generally consumes less energy per tonne-kilometre than freight transport by truck.
FALSO. Energy consumption is generally an advantage of rail: it requires less energy per tonne-kilometre than trucks.
FALSO. In a general comparison, rail is safer than road transport because it has a lower accident rate.
VERO. Rail generally has a lower accident rate than road transport and therefore offers a safety advantage.
FALSO. Rail is not generally the best suited to door-to-door transport: road transport can reach the points of departure and destination more easily.
VERO. Rail generally consumes less energy per tonne-kilometre than road transport and can reduce emissions; the actual benefits depend on the service and the energy used.
It is false that rail is disadvantageous for safety: it is among the safest modes of land transport for freight too.
Rail generally allows lower energy consumption per tonne transported and kilometre than road transport.
Shifting freight from road to sea can reduce traffic and therefore congestion on the road network.
Inland waterways can be improved and integrated into connections with ports. Note: inland navigation is distinct from maritime transport, although it can complete its logistics chain.
If some freight travels by sea instead of by road, road traffic can decrease.
It is false that short sea shipping can never ease congestion: it can carry flows of freight that would otherwise travel by road.
It is false that sea transport is not useful in combined transport: a sea leg can be linked to road or rail legs. The correct term is ‘multimodal’.
It is false that major investment is unnecessary: improving ports, connections with the hinterland and services requires infrastructure work.
It is false that sea transport is always less economical: large quantities of freight can be transported at competitive costs per unit. Cost-effectiveness depends on the route and load, however.
EU security measures for air cargo entail inspection and certification costs for operators; these costs may be passed on to shipments.
It is false that international air freight is prohibited: it is permitted subject to the applicable security checks.
It is false that checks are always quick and have no effect: goods must undergo the required security checks before loading, which may add time.
It is false that logistics access is always adequate: links between an airport and land transport networks may be deficient, slowing the transfer of goods. The situation varies by airport.
It is false that the system is entirely free of fragmentation: European airspace management is fragmented, with effects on cargo flights too. The reference is to air traffic management.
It is false that road transport allows operators to avoid invoicing: ordinary tax obligations apply, depending on the type of transaction.
The quiz treats the specialization of road transport operators as true. The statement is too absolute, however: businesses in other sectors also carry goods on their own account for their own needs.
The stated ranking is false: road transport accounts for the largest share of freight traffic within the EU. The comparison depends on the geographical scope and the indicator used, however.
The opening of the European market has made transport between member states easier and encouraged growth in international road traffic. It is one factor in that growth, not the only cause.
It is false that road transport is always the cheapest method: costs and cost-effectiveness vary with the quantity, distance and organisation of transport.
Goods can be transported by road on own account, for the needs of one's own business, or on behalf of third parties, as a transport service.
A road vehicle can reach places connected to the road network even when they are not served by rail.

On average, maritime transport emits fewer greenhouse gases than road transport per tonne of freight and kilometre. The comparison varies, however, with the ship, the vehicle and the pollutant considered.
Door-to-door service is an advantage of road transport: the vehicle can collect and deliver goods directly at locations served by the road network.
It is false to attribute very high safety levels to road transport compared with all other modes: rail is among the safest forms of land transport.
Road transport offers flexibility in choosing routes and can make direct deliveries, helping provide timely service; actual times also depend on traffic.
The mandatory bracket tariff system has been abolished: the transport charge is left to negotiation between the parties.
International trucks add to the other vehicles on major corridors and contribute to congestion; their contribution relative to other causes varies by place and time.
A return load allows the vehicle to be used on the journey after delivery as well, reducing the kilometres travelled empty.
It is false that road transport does not pollute: vehicles can emit greenhouse gases and air pollutants.
In some cases, road transport allows prompt and efficient service thanks to flexible routes and direct delivery; journey times still depend on travel conditions.
The growth in road freight traffic has contributed to increased emissions from heavy vehicles. The actual trend also depends on efficiency and fuels.
Carrying goods on the return journey too reduces empty trips and makes better use of the vehicle's capacity.
It is false that the loss of human life is insignificant: road accidents, including those involving goods vehicles, can cause deaths and injuries.
A road vehicle can load at the sender's premises and deliver directly to the recipient, if both locations are accessible: this is door-to-door delivery.
Avoiding queues is not a guaranteed advantage: goods vehicles share the road with other users and can get stuck in congestion.
Road transport does not necessarily avoid traffic: the vehicle shares the road with other users and can be delayed.

It is not generally true that road transport pollutes less than rail: per unit of freight transported, rail normally produces fewer greenhouse gas emissions. The comparison depends on the case and the pollutant considered, however.
The road network can directly reach places without rail, port or airport connections, provided they are accessible to the vehicle.
A road vehicle can collect goods from the sender and deliver them directly to the recipient: this is door-to-door service.
Road transport is a predominant mode of land freight transport. Its leading position depends, however, on the geographical scope and the modes included in the comparison.
Flexible routes and direct delivery can make road transport more timely in some cases; the advantage depends on the route and the service used for comparison.
An increase in greenhouse gases is not an advantage: it contributes to climate change and is an environmental impact of transport.

It is false that growth in road freight transport has no effect on the greenhouse effect: other things being equal, more activity using vehicles that produce emissions can increase climate-altering emissions.
It is false that growth has no effect on safety: increased goods vehicle traffic can increase exposure to accident risk, although infrastructure and prevention also matter.
More goods vehicles or more kilometres travelled can increase exposure to accident risk; this does not mean that every increase automatically causes more accidents.

The quiz considers the increase in road freight transport to be true. However, the phrase ‘the last ten years’ does not identify the period, and ‘growth’ may refer to volume or its rate: the result therefore depends on the years and indicator chosen.
It is false that growth has no effect on the environment: greater distances travelled can increase emissions, noise and other impacts, depending on the vehicles and operating conditions.
Combining road, rail and other modes appropriately makes it possible to use the strengths of each and reduce inefficiencies, time or costs depending on the route.
It is false that trans-European networks have no influence: connections and multimodal terminals can encourage more sustainable modes of transport and improve the efficiency of the system.
It is false that logistics is unrelated to sustainability: organizing loads and routes reduces empty trips and can limit fuel consumption and emissions.
FALSO. Sustainable transport is also a European objective: the European Union promotes low-emission vehicles and multimodal transport.
VERO. Intermodality combines different modes of transport and facilitates more efficient and sustainable solutions.
FALSO. The energy used by commercial vehicles also affects sustainability: renewable sources and low-emission fuels can reduce their impact.

VERO. The sustainability of international connections requires cooperation between countries to develop compatible, integrated infrastructure. However, the quiz does not specify a particular mandatory agreement.
VERO. Sustainable transport must also consider and reduce emissions that pollute the air and affect the climate.
FALSO. Maritime transport can be cost-effective in some cases, but it does not guarantee optimization on its own: the choice depends on the route and the needs of the goods.
FALSO. Inland waterway transport is only one option: optimization may require other modes or a combination of them.
VERO. Being able to choose and combine different modes makes it possible to organize transport according to the needs of the route and the goods.
FALSO. Logistics platforms normally bring together several activities and services, such as storage, handling and distribution; the actual services offered vary from one platform to another.
FALSO. Logistics is not limited to particular goods: it organizes flows of different products, with services suited to their characteristics.
VERO. By concentrating and coordinating deliveries, vehicles can be loaded more efficiently and the number of trips reduced, benefiting traffic flow.
FALSO. Logistics does not concern only the physical movement of goods: it also includes the flows of information that accompany the shipment.
VERO. Logistics coordinates flows, storage and distribution, making the organization of transport more efficient.
FALSO. Logistics does not manage only the physical distribution of goods: it also handles the information that accompanies shipments.
FALSO. Logistics can also manage return flows, including packaging and discarded products intended for reuse or disposal.
VERO. The logistics system organizes the transfer and distribution of goods, together with the activities needed along the way.
FALSO. Galileo can help reduce costs: positioning helps organize fleets and routes more efficiently; the savings depend on the application.
FALSO. Galileo provides positioning signals; measuring the pressure in a container requires a specific sensor, which may be connected to a monitoring system.

VERO. A tracking system can use Galileo to locate goods during their journey. ‘At any point’ must be understood within the limits of data reception and transmission: Galileo alone does not send the position to the operator.
FALSO. Galileo is used for positioning and navigation, not for checking every vehicle parameter; other data require dedicated sensors and systems.
VERO. For example, electric trucks often have a higher initial price than equivalent diesel trucks, although they may cost less to operate. The comparison varies by vehicle and market.

VERO. In a typical comparison with a conventional vehicle, a more efficient vehicle uses less fuel to provide the same service. However, not all low-impact vehicles use fuel: electric vehicles use electricity.

FALSO. Low-impact vehicles are relevant because reducing road transport's oil consumption and emissions contributes to sustainability. The 10% share depends on the place and period and is not enough to establish that the impact is negligible.

FALSO. Low environmental impact is often achieved partly through greater energy efficiency: less energy can be used to provide the same service. Actual consumption depends on the vehicle and how it is used.
FALSO. Low-impact vehicles aim to reduce CO2 emissions compared with conventional vehicles; assessing the overall impact also requires considering energy production.
The road transport of dangerous goods is governed by the ADR, subject to the conditions and any exemptions provided for in the agreement.
It is incorrect to say that an invoice must always be on board: the ADR requires the relevant transport documentation, not an invoice in every case.
A generic transport document is not sufficient on its own: when required, it must contain the ADR information on the dangerous goods and be accompanied by the other applicable documents.
The ADR governs the international carriage of dangerous goods by road and sets the conditions for carrying it out.
Fuels classified as dangerous goods, such as diesel, fall under the ADR, subject to any applicable exemptions.
Crude oil is a dangerous good subject to ADR provisions, except for any exemptions provided for.
Controlled temperature for a perishable good does not in itself make it subject to the ADR: the agreement concerns dangerous goods. A good that is also dangerous may nevertheless fall under it.
The transport of oversized work machinery is not ADR transport solely because of that characteristic: the agreement concerns dangerous goods.
Construction materials are not subject to the ADR solely because they are intended for construction: what matters is the classification of the individual goods, which may also be dangerous.
The fact that goods are food does not in itself make the ADR applicable, as it concerns dangerous goods; the classification of the specific product must be checked.
A transport unit can be a motor vehicle on its own or a motor vehicle with a trailer attached: it therefore includes a truck with or without a trailer.
A tractor with a semitrailer attached forms a combination consisting of a motor vehicle and a trailer, and is therefore a transport unit.
A container is an item of transport equipment, not a transport unit: the latter is the motor vehicle, alone or with a trailer attached.
The ADR definition does not include a truck with two trailers: the unit is a motor vehicle alone or with one trailer attached.

The quiz indicates FALSO, considering the tractor without the semitrailer needed to carry the load. The wording is ambiguous, however: the general ADR definition includes a motor vehicle without a trailer attached and does not expressly exclude a tractor on its own.
A detached trailer or semitrailer on its own is not an ADR transport unit: the definition requires a motor vehicle, possibly with a trailer attached.
A bare platform without a superstructure or sides is an example of an open vehicle; the definition also includes platforms fitted with sides.
An open vehicle has a platform without a superstructure, which may be fitted with sides: both configurations described fall within the definition.
A platform fitted with sides can belong to an open vehicle, provided it has no other superstructure.
A vehicle with a closable cargo compartment with rigid walls and roof is an example of a closed vehicle. The ADR definition requires a body that can be closed, without generally specifying rigidity.
A refrigerated or insulated vehicle can be a closed vehicle when it has a body that can be closed: its thermal function does not change this characteristic.
A sheeted vehicle is an open vehicle, which may have sides, on which a sheet protects the load.
A sheeted vehicle is an open vehicle fitted with a sheet that protects the goods carried.
A vehicle with bows supporting the tarpaulin can also be a sheeted vehicle: the tarpaulin protects the load.
A lack of insulation does not make a tank vehicle an open vehicle: an open vehicle is defined by the configuration of its load platform, whereas the tank holds the load.
The tarpaulin identifies a sheeted vehicle: it is an open vehicle fitted with a cover to protect the load.
A van body can be closed and identifies a closed vehicle; it is not an open vehicle.
Sideboards alone do not make a vehicle closed: a closed vehicle has a body that can be closed.
The tarpaulin protects the load of a sheeted vehicle; a closed vehicle, on the other hand, has a body that can be closed.
Bows and a tarpaulin indicate a sheeted covering; they are not enough to define a closed body.
Rigid walls and a rigid roof describe a closed body; a sheeted vehicle, on the other hand, is an open vehicle fitted with a tarpaulin to protect the load.
A sheeted vehicle is not defined as a fireproofed battery vehicle: it is an open vehicle fitted with a tarpaulin to protect the load.
The insulation of a tank does not define a sheeted vehicle, which is an open vehicle with a tarpaulin to protect the load.
For an ordinary flatbed vehicle carrying benzene in packages, no specific ADR suitability annotation is required on the registration certificate.
An annotation on the registration certificate is not generally required to certify suitability for carrying dangerous goods in packages; any specific requirements still apply.
The ATP certificate concerns equipment for transporting perishable foodstuffs; it does not certify ADR suitability for dangerous goods in packages.

The ADR certificate with a pink diagonal stripe is not required for every carriage of goods in packages: it applies to specific categories of vehicles, including those approved for certain explosives.
For ordinary carriage of benzene in packages on a flatbed vehicle, no specific ADR suitability annotation is needed on the registration certificate.
The annotation is not required for an ordinary flatbed vehicle carrying benzene in packages, even solely because the transport is domestic.
No specific ADR suitability annotation is required on the registration certificate for an ordinary flatbed vehicle carrying benzene in packages.

The quiz marks this FALSO: the word “all” does not account for the exceptions provided for some vehicles. A speed limiter is required for N2 and N3 motor vehicles subject to the rules; the date alone is not enough to describe every case.
A retarder is not required on all ADR transport units carrying packages regardless of mass: the requirement depends on the vehicle's category and characteristics.
A speed limiter is required for some motor vehicles, particularly those in categories N2 and N3 subject to the rules, even when they carry goods in packages.
ABS is not required indiscriminately on all ADR transport units carrying packages: the requirements depend on the vehicles' characteristics and registration.
ABS requirements vary according to the vehicle category, mass and date of first registration; the type of ADR transport therefore also matters.
Units subject to ADR provisions must have suitable fire extinguishers; the equipment required varies according to the vehicle and any exemptions.
ADR requires safety equipment for the unit and its crew, with the equipment and any exemptions depending on the transport operation.
Special electrical equipment is not always required for ADR transport in packages: the requirements depend on the type of vehicle and transport.

In the ordinary case of packages other than explosives and radioactive materials, no specific ADR certificate of vehicle suitability is required. This does not eliminate any other documents required for the transport.
An indivisible beam projecting beyond the front outline of the truck constitutes exceptional transport; the relevant authorization is required.
For a standalone truck, the ordinary length limit, including the load, is 12 metres: exceeding it constitutes transport under exceptional conditions.
Transport is under exceptional conditions when the indivisible beam causes the vehicle to exceed the dimensional limits set by the Highway Code, including the length limit.

A rear projection of 20% does not in itself make the transport exceptional: what matters is whether the overall dimensional limit is exceeded. For an indivisible load, the rear projection limit must also be respected.
A rear projection of 10% is not enough to define the transport as exceptional: it is necessary to check whether the vehicle and load exceed the dimensional limit.
A projection of one quarter of the length does not automatically make the transport exceptional: the overall length must be checked against the dimensional limit.
The transport of an indivisible item is under exceptional conditions when its dimensions cause the vehicle to exceed the dimensional limits set by the Highway Code.
Eleven metres is not the ordinary threshold: for a standalone truck, the length limit, including the load, is 12 metres. Exceeding 11 metres is therefore not enough to make the transport exceptional.
A rear projection alone does not always make the transport exceptional: an indivisible beam may project within the prescribed limits without exceeding the vehicle's dimensional limit.

For transport subject to the European regulation, the documents on board state, among other things, the origin, destination and expected duration of the journey. The word “always” is too broad, however: the regulation excludes, for example, transport unrelated to an economic activity.
ADR does not concern only maritime transport: it is the agreement on the international carriage of dangerous goods by road.

Businesses transporting waste are normally required to register in the relevant category of the National Register of Environmental Operators. There are specific exceptions, however, for example for certain transport of their own waste by agricultural entrepreneurs.

Registration in the Register of Road Hauliers is not enough: registration in the National Register of Environmental Operators is normally also required for waste transport, subject to the prescribed exceptions.
Metallurgical waste does not fall under ATP as such: the agreement concerns the transport of certain perishable foodstuffs and the special equipment used.
Dangerous goods do not fall under ATP because of their dangerous nature: ATP concerns certain perishable foodstuffs and the associated special equipment.
It does not apply only to international journeys: in Italy, ATP requirements also apply to domestic transport of certain foodstuffs, such as frozen foods.
ATP is not the agreement on dangerous goods: it concerns the transport of perishable foodstuffs and the special equipment used.
ATP does not mean authorization to transport agricultural products: it refers to the agreement on the transport of perishable foodstuffs and the special equipment to be used.
ATP refers to the international agreement on the transport of perishable foodstuffs and the special equipment to be used for that transport.
ATP rules concern certain perishable foodstuffs and the special equipment used to transport them, not all food products indiscriminately.

It is incorrect to rule out approval: a modification to an insulated body may require inspection and testing and an update to the registration certificate. The specific procedure depends on the modification.

The quiz marks this FALSO because a simple notification does not cover all the formalities: the fitting requires the applicable checks and approval. The statement is ambiguous because it does not expressly say that notification alone is sufficient.
The fact that the vehicle is already in use does not eliminate the formalities: fitting the body requires the prescribed checks and updates to the documents.
Special waste is not subject to ATP simply because it is waste: the agreement concerns certain perishable foodstuffs and the special equipment for transporting them.
ATP does not mean authorization to transport petroleum products: it is the agreement on the transport of perishable foodstuffs and the special equipment used for it.
The ATP agreement concerns the transport of perishable foodstuffs and sets requirements for the special equipment used for this purpose.
ATP concerns the transport of certain perishable foodstuffs and the special equipment used, not dangerous goods as such.
ATP governs the transport of certain perishable foodstuffs, not the transport of waste as such.
ATP concerns certain perishable foodstuffs, not goods identified by their ability to contaminate water.
Non-perishable food does not require an ATP vehicle simply because it is food; hygiene requirements still apply, such as cleaning and maintaining the load compartment.
Not all food requires an ATP vehicle: the agreement concerns certain perishable foodstuffs and specific transport conditions.
Hygiene requirements also apply to non-perishable food: for example, the load compartment must be cleaned and maintained so as to protect it from contamination.
It is false that an ATP vehicle is never mandatory: for perishable foodstuffs and transport covered by the agreement, equipment complying with the prescribed conditions must be used.
ATP vehicle bodies are not exclusively mechanically refrigerated: the agreement also distinguishes insulated, refrigerated and heated equipment, according to its characteristics and intended use.

The VIN plate identifies the vehicle and is not the marking that proves the body's ATP compliance. ATP instead provides for a certificate of compliance and specific markings; this does not rule out the vehicle also having a VIN.
The vehicle's compliance with ATP rules is certified by a certificate issued by the competent authority, following the checks required by the agreement.
Bodies for perishable foodstuffs are classified according to ATP categories, not ADR, which concerns the transport of dangerous goods.
An ATP vehicle is not required for non-perishable food products simply because it carries food; the applicable hygiene rules still apply.

A significant modification to the body may require inspection and approval, including an inspection and test at the UMC and an update to the documents. The actual procedure depends on the modification: not every minor intervention automatically entails the same procedure.
Frozen products are among the foodstuffs governed by ATP, which specifies temperature conditions and the choice of equipment for them.
When opening the vehicle, even for an inspection, care must be taken not to expose the foodstuffs to conditions that compromise compliance with temperature requirements or their safety or quality.

The quiz marks this false because the permitted tolerance is up to 3 °C, not 2 °C. The wording is ambiguous, however: a 2 °C increase still falls within the permitted maximum during the specified operations and under the prescribed conditions.
During certain operations, such as defrosting the evaporator, a brief increase of up to 3 °C may be allowed on the surface of foodstuffs in part of the load.
The quiz marks this false because the tolerance limit is 3 °C, not 1 °C. The statement is ambiguous, however: a 1 °C increase falls within the permitted maximum if the prescribed conditions are met.
The temperature of the foodstuff must stay within the prescribed maximum at every point in the load, subject to the specific operational tolerances permitted by ATP.
The rule concerns the highest temperature, which must not exceed the product's limit at any point in the load; it does not require the lowest temperature to remain above that limit.

Checks must not be limited to the central area: the limit applies at every point in the load. The statement is ambiguous because, taken on its own, the condition concerning the centre is still included in the general rule.
The limit applies not only to the side area but to every point in the load. The statement is ambiguous because the condition concerning the side area is still included in the general rule.
A partnership can also carry out road haulage for hire or reward, provided it meets the requirements and holds the required registrations; its legal form does not prohibit this.
In the context of the quiz, carriers are normally private businesses that transport goods for customers; this does not rule out other organizational forms.
A transport business can have different sizes and legal forms: for example, it can be a sole proprietorship or a company, subject to the requirements for access to the profession.
A carrier can take the form of a joint-stock company, provided it meets the requirements to carry out transport.
A company with share capital is not mandatory: transport can also be carried out by a sole proprietor.
A limited liability company can carry out road transport if it meets the required conditions; its legal form does not exclude it.
There is no requirement for maritime transport to predominate: modes are chosen and combined according to the route and the needs of the service.
Inland waterway transport does not necessarily predominate: the choice combines the modes best suited to the route and the service.
Road transport does not necessarily predominate: the network combines several modes according to the route and the needs of the service.
The choice and combination of available modes affect the costs and management of the transport network.
Registration in the road hauliers' register is required to carry out road haulage of goods for hire or reward.
Professional goods transport in vehicles requiring a C1 or C licence normally requires a goods CQC. The question does not mention the exemptions for particular uses.
The company's registration in the register does not exempt its employees: when the transport falls within the scope of the rules, they must comply with driving times, breaks and rest periods.
It is wrong to exclude the legal entity: both the party that assumes the company's relationships and obligations and the party that directs its economic decisions must be considered.
Organization matters: people, vehicles and activities must be coordinated to provide the transport service.
The type of transport affects the organization: different goods and services may require different vehicles, equipment and procedures.
It is wrong to exclude the economic decision-maker: both the party that assumes rights and obligations and the party that directs the company's economic decisions matter to its organization.
It is wrong to say that only the type of transport matters: size, resources and desired responsibilities can also influence the choice of company form.
It is wrong to exclude the legal form: it affects the structure of the business, for example the relationships between partners and their responsibilities.
In subcontracted transport, the carrier contracts another carrier to perform the transport, or part of it.
The work is entrusted to the subcontracting carrier under a contract; the absence of a written form does not necessarily mean there is no contract.
A fuel cell uses hydrogen to produce electricity, which can power the vehicle's electric motor.

The quiz considers CNG, LPG and LNG alternative fuels useful in the transition. The phrase 'cannot do without' is absolute, however: their use is not indispensable to every development of electric and hybrid mobility.
Diesel is not indispensable to the development of sustainable mobility: electric propulsion and other energy carriers also exist.
Petrol and diesel are not the specific infrastructure needed by electric vehicles: rechargeable vehicles need charging points; other alternative vehicles need their respective refuelling facilities.
LPG is stored in liquid form under relatively moderate pressure. The 6–8 bar figure is indicative: pressure varies with temperature and the composition of the mixture.
CNG is not stored at only 6–8 bar: compressed natural gas is stored on board at high pressure, around 200 bar.
High-pressure natural gas cylinders may be used to fuel the engine, provided the system meets type-approval requirements.
The gas system may be fitted by the manufacturer or installed through a later conversion, in accordance with the applicable requirements.
A bi-fuel system allows a choice between petrol and a gaseous fuel, either LPG or natural gas, using one fuel at a time.
In a dual-fuel system, natural gas and diesel are used together: a quantity of diesel helps ignite the natural gas.

In the sense usually intended by the quiz, natural gas dual-fuel also uses diesel to help ignition, not a natural gas–LPG mixture. The term dual-fuel on its own, however, means the use of two fuels and does not necessarily identify just one pair.

The quiz marks this FALSO, referring to the common petrol–LPG and petrol–natural gas combinations. The wording is too absolute, however: tri-fuel vehicles that also allow a choice between LPG and natural gas are technically possible.
Biomethane made from organic residues is renewable, but its actual sustainability depends on production and emissions management throughout the supply chain.
It is wrong to consider it necessarily highly polluting: biomethane comes from renewable organic material, although its impact depends on the supply chain and any leaks.
30% is an approximate order of magnitude for a conventional engine: much energy is lost, mainly as heat. Actual efficiency varies with the engine and operating conditions.

60% is not the approximate figure sought by the quiz: for a conventional engine, about 30% is assumed, with variations depending on the engine and conditions; the remainder includes substantial heat losses.
The motor uses electrical energy and electromagnetic fields to produce mechanical motion, which is transmitted to the wheels.
Petrol and diesel are two fuels for combustion engines: using both does not define electric propulsion. A hybrid vehicle, on the other hand, combines an electric motor with a combustion engine.
Methane and LPG are fuels for a combustion engine: any combination of the two does not power an electric motor, which requires electrical energy.
A rechargeable lithium-ion battery can supply electrical energy to the traction motor.
Rechargeable lead-acid batteries can also power electric propulsion; in current commercial electric vehicles, they are used mainly for auxiliary functions.
The quiz indicates VERO because batteries have a limited lifespan and may need replacing. However, there is no universal fixed interval: the need depends on the battery's condition and lifespan.
Charging is not necessarily very quick: the time depends, among other things, on the battery's capacity, its charge level and the available power.
A fully electric vehicle does not need a petrol tank, so it does not require one to be replaced periodically. A hybrid, however, may have a tank.
Electric conversion is provided for certain categories of vehicles, using compliant systems and following the established conditions and procedures.
AVAS produces an audible signal to make an electric or hybrid vehicle easier to notice, especially at low speeds, protecting vulnerable road users such as pedestrians.
AVAS is not intended to protect buses from cars moving away: it audibly alerts vulnerable road users to the presence of electric or hybrid vehicles, particularly at low speeds.
The stated ban does not exist: electric heavy vehicles are mass-produced.
In fuel cells, hydrogen enables electricity to be produced on board, powering the electric traction motor.
It is wrong to say there are no problems: hydrogen's low volumetric density makes transport and storage challenging and expensive, requiring suitable systems.
Hydrogen vehicles are subject to technical type-approval requirements, including those relating to the system and components that contain hydrogen.
It is not true that such vehicles are excluded: hydrogen can also power an internal combustion engine, in addition to being used in fuel cells.
The cell uses an electrochemical reaction to convert the chemical energy of hydrogen into electrical energy.
The direction of conversion is reversed: the fuel cell produces electricity from the chemical energy of the fuel. Producing hydrogen using electricity, on the other hand, is electrolysis.

In the operation considered by the quiz, fuel cells for vehicle propulsion run on hydrogen, not directly on diesel. The question is ambiguous, however: diesel can be converted into a hydrogen-rich gas using a reformer.
Oxygen is not the fuel: in the cell it reacts with hydrogen, which is the fuel.
The individual cells are connected in series in a stack; the size and number of cells depend on the required electrical performance.

The quiz rules out a tank made entirely of plastic: pressure-resistant containers, often made of composite materials, are used for compressed hydrogen. The wording is ambiguous because some have an inner polymer lining.
At ambient temperature and pressure, hydrogen has little energy per unit of volume, so it takes up more space than common liquid fuels for the same amount of energy.
The quiz considers the absence of emissions due to carbon in the fuel: hydrogen contains no carbon. This does not mean zero pollutant emissions: combustion with air can produce nitrogen oxides.
It cannot be claimed that a hydrogen engine is much more polluting: hydrogen contains no carbon, and its combustion does not directly generate CO₂ from the fuel. It can still produce nitrogen oxides.
A hybrid combines combustion and electric propulsion and can manage them differently depending on its configuration and driving conditions.

In some hybrids, propulsion can be provided by the electric motor or the combustion engine, including separately. However, the ability to drive on electric power alone depends on the architecture: it does not apply to every hybrid.
It is not true that hybrids use only the combustion engine: the electric system can contribute to propulsion and, in some configurations, provide it alone.
The combustion engine can drive a generator that produces electricity for the electric system, powering the traction motor or charging the battery.
In a series hybrid, propulsion is electric; the vehicle also has a battery and a combustion engine that supplies electrical energy through a generator.
The direct connection of both motors to the wheels describes a parallel hybrid. In a series hybrid, the wheels are driven by the electric motor.
In the parallel arrangement considered, the electric motor works with the combustion engine, which remains part of the drivetrain; the proportions of their contributions depend on the design.
The two motors do not always have to operate together: a series-parallel system can use different modes depending on driving conditions.
During braking, the electric machine can act as a generator: it recovers some of the energy of motion and sends it to the battery.
The combustion engine is not used exclusively for direct propulsion: it can also drive a generator that powers the electric system.
In the split type intended by the quiz, the combustion engine and electric motor drive different axles, providing four-wheel drive. The term split can also refer to other hybrid architectures.
When operating as a motor, the electric machine receives electrical energy and converts it into mechanical energy to move the vehicle.
Operation as a motor is confused with operation as a generator: when electrically powered, the machine provides propulsion; to recharge, it instead recovers mechanical energy.
During regenerative braking, the electric machine can act as a generator, converting some of the energy of motion into electricity for the battery.

In the comparison assumed by the quiz, the hybrid's emissions are about 53% of those of the gasoline engine, so the reduction is about 47%, not 53%. Energy recovery and less use of the combustion engine can reduce fuel consumption and emissions; the figure is not universal and depends on the comparison and use.

The quiz gives 53%, not 10%, of the gasoline engine's emissions in the comparison assumed. This is an exam estimate, not a percentage valid for every hybrid and every route: the result also depends on how the vehicle is used.
In the European Union, transport accounts for about a quarter of total greenhouse gas emissions. The share depends on the area and period considered.
Encouraging the adoption of zero- or low-emission vehicles helps reduce the impact of transport and supports the transition to sustainable mobility.
Accessible charging and refuelling points make it possible to use vehicles powered by alternative energy and fuels and encourage their adoption.
Sustainable mobility also concerns the use of resources: designing, reusing and recycling vehicles and components applies circular economy principles to the sector.
It is wrong to say there is no link: the adoption of zero- or low-emission vehicles is one of the measures that support sustainable mobility.
It is wrong to say that the transition is independent of infrastructure: charging and refuelling points enable the use and encourage the adoption of alternatively powered vehicles.
Electric heavy vehicles can contribute to sustainable mobility because they produce no exhaust emissions while driving; the overall impact also depends on how the energy is produced.
It is wrong to say there are no effects: electric heavy vehicles produce no exhaust emissions while driving and can help reduce the impact of transport.
Allocating resources to goods vehicles powered by cleaner alternatives can help renew the vehicle fleet and reduce the impact of transport. The benefit depends on the fuel and its production cycle.
It is not irrelevant: supporting the purchase of goods vehicles using alternative fuels can help the transition, provided that the actual impact of the fuel used is considered.
Resources can also be conserved for longer in transport: vehicle components and materials can be recovered, reused or recycled.
It is wrong to exclude goods transport: logistics can also organize the return flows of products and materials intended for reuse and recovery.
Logistics hubs can participate in the circular economy, for example by organizing the return and consolidation of goods and materials intended for reuse or recovery.
Vehicle design can make repair, dismantling, component reuse and material recycling easier: in this way, the circular economy also involves goods vehicles.
There are heavy vehicles powered by compressed natural gas, CNG, and others powered by liquefied natural gas, LNG. The two forms require different storage systems.
Hydrogen can also help decarbonize transport, for example by powering fuel cells. The overall result also depends on how the hydrogen is produced.
It is wrong to exclude hydrogen: it can power fuel-cell trucks and help decarbonization, especially if produced with low emissions.
Hydrogen can power fuel-cell trucks and help decarbonize goods transport. The overall benefit also depends on emissions from its production.
It is wrong to consider this technology irrelevant: fuel cells convert the energy in hydrogen into electricity for propulsion and can be used in both light and heavy vehicles.
There are dual-fuel heavy vehicles whose engines use natural gas together with diesel, which helps ignite the mixture.

The quiz considers the economic advantage true: replacing some diesel with natural gas can reduce costs. However, relative prices vary over time and by location, so savings are not guaranteed and must be compared for the same amount of energy or distance traveled.
LNG is liquefied natural gas: in a dual-fuel system it is stored as a liquid in a cryogenic tank kept at a very low temperature.
It is wrong to speak of gaseous storage in ordinary cylinders: LNG is stored as a liquid in cryogenic tanks; cylinders for compressed natural gas are used for CNG.

The quiz considers the possible environmental advantage of dual-fuel systems true: some vehicles can be quieter and reduce certain emissions. This is not automatic, however: it depends on the vehicle and conditions; methane emissions must also be considered.

It is wrong to claim that dual-fuel vehicles are necessarily noisier and more polluting: in some tests, vehicles were quieter. However, emissions and noise depend on the vehicle and its use, and methane leaks can worsen the climate impact.
Anticipatory driving requires observing the road and anticipating possible hazards so that maneuvers can be prepared in good time.
Pitching can affect stability: under braking, load transfers forward and the rear wheels may have less grip.
The softness and flexibility of the suspension affect the vehicle's longitudinal oscillating response, including pitching.
It is more than a nuisance: during pitching, the load on the wheels changes and, for example, heavy braking can reduce rear grip.
Pitching accompanies changes in speed that can destabilize the vehicle and shift the load and passengers; the risk depends on the severity of the maneuver and the restraints in place.

The quiz considers it false to attribute pitching to tire wear: longitudinal oscillation is mainly linked to load transfers, suspension and shock absorbers. Wear can still affect other aspects of vehicle dynamics and safety and should not be considered irrelevant to driving.
Pitching is a longitudinal oscillation, not a force that opposes centrifugal force. When cornering, it is roll that tilts the vehicle sideways.
The wording is imprecise: risks are anticipated by observing the road, not by braking. Anticipating them then allows gradual braking under normal conditions.
Pitching is the forward and backward oscillation of the body around a transverse axis passing through the center of gravity.
Anticipatory driving does not mean braking abruptly: the driver observes ahead and normally brakes in good time and gradually. In an emergency, immediate braking may be necessary.

There is no rule that pitching always decreases as rear overhang increases. The oscillation also depends on mass distribution, suspension and shock absorbers: overhang alone does not determine the result.
Pitching causes forward and backward oscillations that can be unpleasant for passengers and upset the vehicle's balance.
The point of the quiz is that passengers also feel the deceleration. More precisely, the brakes act on the vehicle, which slows the passengers through seats, seat belts or other contact points.
Coasting in neutral is not anticipatory driving: it eliminates engine braking and can reduce control. The driver approaches while anticipating the stop and adjusting speed in good time.
It is wrong to say that passengers are unaffected by braking: the vehicle slows them through contact with seats, seat belts or handholds, and sudden braking can make them fall.
Roll also depends on the suspension: its stiffness and damping affect the tilt and lateral oscillations of the vehicle body.
Driving behavior affects roll: a sudden steering movement rapidly changes the lateral distribution of the load and can increase the tilt.
Closely spaced bends can amplify roll if the second force is applied before the first oscillation has died down; the effect also depends on speed and the sequence of bends.
Excessive roll can reduce the load on the inner wheels until they lift off the ground and, in the most severe cases, lead to a rollover.
Roll is not necessarily stabilizing: the sideways tilt can cause an inadequately secured load to shift and increase the risk of rollover.
When cornering, the tires must already provide lateral grip: sudden braking can exceed the available grip and cause a skid.
Braking does not reduce the load on the front axle: it transfers load toward the front, reducing the load on the rear.
Sudden braking can make passengers lose their balance or hit parts of the bus, causing injuries.
During sudden braking, goods tend to continue moving forward due to inertia; if they are not securely fastened, they can shift dangerously.
Frequent sudden braking puts more strain on the brakes and heats them more, accelerating their wear.
FALSO. When braking while traveling forward, an unsecured load tends due to inertia to move forward relative to the vehicle, not backward.
FALSO. Under braking, the vehicle tends to pitch forward: the load on the front axle increases, while the load on the rear axle decreases.
FALSO. Braking transfers load toward the front axle and reduces the load on the rear axle rather than overloading it.
FALSO. A motorway must have at least two traffic lanes on each carriageway, not necessarily three.
FALSO. State roads belong to the state; municipal roads belong to the municipality.
VERO. Connecting the municipality's main town with its outlying settlements is one of the criteria for municipal roads outside built-up areas.
FALSO. Motorways are reserved for certain categories: for example, mopeds are not allowed on them.

FALSO. Motorways and major roads outside built-up areas are technical and functional categories; the administrative classification instead distinguishes state, regional, provincial and municipal roads.
FALSO. Provincial is an administrative classification and does not guarantee the absence of at-grade intersections: that feature is required, for example, on motorways.
VERO. One of the criteria for regional roads outside built-up areas is that they connect provincial capitals within the same region.
FALSO. A state road does not have to cross at least three regions: it may be classified as such, for example, because it forms a major national traffic route.
VERO. The Highway Code defines a road as an area for public use intended for the movement of pedestrians, vehicles and animals.

FALSO under the quiz's classification criteria: connecting the capitals of different regions is listed among the criteria for state roads. This does not rule out a regional road crossing a regional boundary.

A waiting room, ticket office and café are public services normally associated with the passenger building; the vehicle building serves the buses.
The vehicle building can bring together the services buses need, such as storage, parking, cleaning and refuelling.
The vehicle building is normally an operational space for storage and maintenance, separate from the waiting areas accessible to passengers.
The vehicle building can include a workshop and equipped spaces for bus maintenance and repairs.
Cafés, newsstands and other commercial services are intended for passengers; they are not the function of the vehicle building, which is reserved for bus services.

The quiz considers it false that height is a cause of danger in itself. The wording is broad, however: what matters is that the driver can see and reach the controls properly, including by adjusting the driving position.
Organised stops and bus stations can make bus operations and movements more orderly, helping services keep to schedule; the benefit depends on their design and management.
The quiz considers it false that age is a cause of danger in itself. The wording is broad: the driver's fitness and actual abilities remain relevant to safe driving.
The quiz distinguishes contractual conditions from immediate dangers while driving. The wording is broad: working conditions that cause fatigue can still affect safety.
Well-designed stops and bus stations organise boarding, alighting and bus movements, reducing interference and operational time. The actual benefits depend on their design and use.

It is wrong to claim that these facilities necessarily increase the environmental impact of vehicles: well-organized stops and bus stations can make the service more orderly. The actual effect also depends on their design and use.
It is incorrect to rule out benefits for mobility: stops and bus stations organise access to services and transfers between passengers and buses.
Rain and ice can reduce grip, while fog limits visibility: speed must be adjusted to the conditions.
Bends, crests and junctions can restrict visibility or create conflicts with other road users; speed must be reduced.
The quiz indicates FALSO, but the wording is ambiguous: vehicle characteristics can affect risk and require an appropriate speed. The type of vehicle is not in itself synonymous with danger.
Excessive speed increases the distance needed to stop and can make it impossible to avoid an obstacle.
Stops and bus stations can serve different categories of public transport vehicles, depending on the characteristics and intended use of the facility.
A pedestrian who does not know the rules may, for example, cross unexpectedly or dangerously. Knowing and following the rules helps reduce the risk.
A careless crossing or a maneuver that fails to respect right of way can create a danger for other road users.
It is wrong to consider the mere presence of road signs dangerous: signs guide road users and regulate traffic.
A dedicated lane can make the journey smoother, reducing time spent in queues and improving comfort; the benefit depends on conditions along the route.

A reserved lane can make traffic flow more smoothly and reduce braking and restarting caused by traffic, limiting wear on some components. The benefit depends on the actual conditions of the lane and service.
By avoiding some queues, dedicated lanes help services run regularly and keep to schedule, without guaranteeing this in every situation.
It is incorrect to say that dedicated lanes necessarily create greater risks: they separate traffic or reduce interference with ordinary traffic, although care is still needed at crossing points.
Smoother travel can reduce stops and starts, fuel consumption and emissions; the effect depends on traffic and the vehicle.
‘Never’ is incorrect: other vehicles may pass through the area when permitted; parking in reserved spaces remains prohibited.
A bus bay does not in itself cause congestion: it allows the vehicle to stop outside the carriageway, leaving the lane clearer.
The stop is identified by a stop post or a specific upright sign, so that passengers and other road users can recognise it.
Yellow zigzag lines can mark the space a bus needs to pull in and move off again.
The bay includes space to manoeuvre into the stop and rejoin traffic.
Blue is incorrect: the lines marking the stop are yellow.
A stop does not normally need to be bounded by kerbs: its boundary can be marked with yellow lines on the road surface.
It is wrong to say that the bay is within the carriageway: it is a part of the road outside the carriageway, intended for scheduled-service vehicles to stop.
The quiz indicates VERO: the areas before and after the stop are used for manoeuvring. Note that zigzag lines can mark them, but are not mandatory in every case.
Blue is incorrect: when the stop boundary is marked, yellow lines are used.
The quiz indicates VERO because the word BUS is prescribed in the stopping area. To clarify: the yellow line marks the boundary of the area; the word is placed inside it.
The bay is a part of the road outside the carriageway, intended for scheduled public transport vehicles to stop.
It is the opposite: parking is prohibited in stopping areas; a brief stop may be permitted if it does not cause an obstruction and no other restrictions apply.
The prohibition applies to parking, not necessarily to a brief stop, which remains subject to other restrictions and must not obstruct the service.
When present, the road markings defining the stop use yellow lines.
Parking cars is prohibited; a brief stop may be permitted if it causes no obstruction and no other restrictions apply.
The stated colour is incorrect: the broken longitudinal line is yellow, not light blue.
The stop is identified by a specific upright sign; the boundaries of the space can also be indicated by road markings.
When the boundary is marked on the road, the lines are yellow.
The road marking defining the stop is yellow, not white.
The word ‘always’ is incorrect: yellow zigzag lines can mark the areas used for manoeuvring, but are not mandatory in every case.
The bay is outside the carriageway: the bus can pull in without occupying the traffic lane, helping traffic flow.
A shelter may be provided, but it is not mandatory at every stop.
The word BUS is prescribed inside the stopping area marked on the road surface.
The wording given is incorrect: the word BUS is prescribed on the road surface.
The bay is intended for public transport vehicles to stop, not for other vehicles to park.
It is not true that an upright sign is always absent: the stop is identified by a specific sign.
It is not true that yellow lines are never used: they are prescribed for marking the stop on the road surface.
Private vehicles may be allowed to pass through when the stop occupies part of the carriageway open to traffic, provided they obey the signs and do not obstruct the service.
The stop is intended for scheduled public transport vehicles, to allow passengers to board and alight.
True. A stop may be near spaces for other transport services, making transfers easier; each space retains its intended use.
The stop is not closed to the public: it is where passengers board and leave the vehicle.
When several routes serve the same stop area, passengers can get off one vehicle and continue on another, making transfers easier.
The stop allows passengers to board the bus and thus access the service.
A stop may have a pedestrian refuge, a protected space where pedestrians can shelter and wait.
A general danger sign does not identify the stop: the appropriate stop sign is used instead.
The statement reverses the roles: the sign is installed by the service operator after agreement with the authority that owns the road.
The stop is marked by an appropriate sign; a flashing yellow light does not identify it.
The stop sign may also display service timetables, possibly on a supplementary panel.
For stops outside built-up areas, the BUS STOP or TRAM STOP sign is used, depending on the service.
The service operator installs the sign after agreement with the authority that owns the road.
Parking cars in the space reserved for the stop is prohibited even outside service hours: the rule makes no such exception.
The two outer sections of the stopping area are each 12 m long and are used for entry and exit maneuvers.
The central section does not have a fixed length of 12 m: it must be at least as long as the longest vehicle that stops there, plus 2 m.
The central section of the area must be at least as long as the longest vehicle that stops there, plus 2 m; the rule applies to this section, in addition to the maneuvering areas.
The first section of the stopping area is used to pull up to the curb; the last is used to rejoin traffic.
Being five meters from the sign does not permit parking in the reserved area. If the space is not marked out, the prohibition applies within 15 m of the sign.
The prescribed minimum is 50 m, not 70 m. The official answer is FALSO because 70 m is not mandatory; an actual distance of 70 m would nevertheless meet the minimum.
On these roads, the stops on the two sides must be at least 50 m apart and staggered according to their respective directions of travel.
Thirty meters is not enough: the prescribed minimum distance between the stops is 50 m.
Forty meters is not enough: the prescribed minimum distance between the stops is 50 m.
The general rule requires vehicles to travel on the right-hand side of the carriageway, close to the right edge.
There is no general ban on reversing in built-up areas based on that weight. The maneuver must be performed safely, giving way to vehicles traveling normally.
A weight over 7.5 t does not in itself entail that ban: vehicles may travel on tracks at road level without obstructing or slowing trams, unless signs indicate otherwise.
The rule is to use the rightmost free lane; in built-up areas, drivers may also choose the appropriate lane for the direction they intend to take at the next intersection.
The bus is more than 7 m long: unless signs indicate otherwise, it may use only the two lanes closest to the right edge, even if it weighs less than 5 t.
The goods vehicle exceeds 5 t: unless signs indicate otherwise, it must use only the two lanes closest to the right edge.
Unless signs indicate otherwise, drivers use the rightmost free lane, and the lanes to the left are reserved for overtaking; in built-up areas, the rules for the next intersection also apply.
If the road has two separate carriageways, drivers use the one on the right.
The right lane is not reserved solely for entering and exiting: it is normally the lane to use when free.
The weight limit over 5 t applies to goods vehicles; this bus is less than 7 m long. It may therefore use the left lane when the other rules allow it.
The right lane is not reserved solely for slow vehicles: the general rule requires drivers to use the rightmost free lane, unless signs indicate otherwise.

Passing on the right is not prohibited: if the pedestrian refuge is to the right of the road's center line, vehicles may pass on either side, unless signs indicate otherwise, while staying in the part allocated to their direction of travel and without obstructing passengers.

A length over 7 meters does not require a vehicle to remain in the right lane at all times on a carriageway with two lanes in each direction. The general rule of using the rightmost free lane applies, with the option of using the other lane when permitted, for example to overtake.
Travel in parallel lines is also permitted when authorized by traffic officers.
There is no general ban on travel in parallel lines based on a weight of 12 tonnes. What matters is that the prescribed conditions for such travel are met or that traffic officers authorize it.

With only one lane in each direction, there is normally no room for two lines traveling in the same direction. The verdict needs qualification, however: Article 144 also permits travel in parallel lines when authorized by traffic officers.

In built-up areas, on a carriageway with at least two lanes in each direction, drivers may choose the lane best suited to the direction they intend to take at the next intersection, while obeying the signs.
A length over 12 meters alone does not prohibit travel in parallel lines: the prescribed conditions for such travel or authorization from traffic officers must be respected.

The official verdict is false because the type of service is not always the decisive factor in assessing risk while driving: the actual conditions and the driver's behavior matter. The wording is ambiguous, however, because the service provided can affect risks and passenger comfort.
Not every dangerous situation can always be avoided. The driver must anticipate them as far as possible and increase safety margins by driving appropriately.

The driver's relationship with colleagues is not always decisive in assessing immediate risk while driving; attention should focus mainly on traffic, the road and the driver's condition. The statement is broad, however: cooperation can be relevant in some work situations.
It is wrong to exclude starting and braking: these too should be as gradual as possible to avoid jolts and improve passenger safety and comfort.
Attention makes it possible to notice changes and hazards in good time; distraction can impair the driver's risk assessment and response.
Proper and responsible conduct protects other road users: the driver must avoid creating danger or obstruction and safeguard traffic safety.
Prudent driving avoids adding risks and helps prevent dangerous situations, although it cannot guarantee that every external hazard can be avoided.
Braking early and moderately when conditions permit makes deceleration smoother and reduces the jolts felt by passengers.
Anticipating maneuvers in good time allows them to be performed gradually when conditions permit, limiting sudden movements for passengers.
Experience helps the driver recognize and assess hazards, together with attention and the ability to react.
Educational qualifications are not in themselves always decisive in assessing risks. Training, experience, attention and the ability to recognize hazards are important when driving.
It is false that a driver's behavior cannot counter danger: observing, anticipating and adapting one's driving can increase safety margins.

The composition of the entire vehicle fleet is not always decisive for the risk encountered on a single drive; the characteristics of the vehicle used and the actual conditions also matter. The wording is ambiguous because fleet composition can affect the company's risk assessment.
It is false that a driver's physical condition never causes danger: for example, fatigue can reduce attention and alertness. The driver must be fit to drive.
Safety devices help reduce risks or consequences, but they cannot guarantee that every danger will be avoided. Attention and adapting one's driving remain necessary.
Reaction speed affects the time needed to act after recognising a danger. Drivers must therefore remain attentive and maintain adequate safety margins.
The driver must recognise and deal with dangers by taking appropriate action to protect people and increase safety margins.
Keeping the speed as steady as possible limits the acceleration and deceleration felt by passengers. Speed must still be adapted to road and traffic conditions.
It is false that a driver can never deal with a danger: attention, an appropriate speed and timely manoeuvres can allow the driver to react safely.
Safety devices help prevent or limit the consequences of an accident, but they do not eliminate every danger: the driver must still drive carefully.
The driver must drive in a way that protects passengers, maintaining control of the vehicle and avoiding dangerous manoeuvres.
A speed suited to the radius of the bend limits the sideways forces on passengers and contributes to a safe and comfortable journey.
Before departure, the driver checks that the fire extinguishers are present and that their periodic inspections are up to date.
The bus must have the required interior lighting in passenger compartments and entrance and exit areas so that they can be used safely.
The required interior lighting must be present and working: a faulty system does not ensure the visibility needed on board.
The quiz considers the 12-month interval false: the periodic inspection is every six months. Note that servicing the fire extinguisher is separate from inspection and has its own interval.
Before departure, the driver checks that the required fire extinguishers are on board and available in case of fire.
It is false that interior lighting is not mandatory: it is required in passenger compartments and entrance and exit areas.
It is false that it is not checked: the vehicle inspection includes an examination of the interior lighting and identifies any defects or failures.

The quiz considers false the idea that interior lighting is required only on some buses: it is required in passenger compartments. The statement is ambiguous, however, because 'may be present on some' is literally compatible with being present on all of them.
Before departure, the windows, mirrors and indirect vision devices must be checked to ensure they are clean and working properly, giving the driver an adequate view.
The driver checks that the warning triangle is on board so that it can be used to signal the stationary vehicle when required.
The driver checks the date shown on the fire extinguisher: the periodic inspection must be carried out at least every six months.
Before departure, the presence of the required wheel chocks is checked; they help prevent accidental movement of the stationary vehicle.
If the safety windows require hammers, their presence must be checked so the windows can be broken in an emergency.
The interior lighting must be checked periodically for faults; it is also checked during the vehicle inspection.
The quiz considers it false that this check applies as a general bus equipment requirement: rear panels for heavy vehicles apply to specific categories, including goods vehicles, and not all buses.
The panel is not equipment that must always be checked on a bus: it is used to mark a load projecting from the rear when there is one.
Before departure, the presence of the required first aid kit is checked; it is needed to provide initial assistance on board.
Before departure, the presence of the required first aid kit is checked; it is needed to provide initial assistance on board.
Compliance with emission limits is necessary, but it is not established by a measurement before every departure: instrument testing is part of the periodic vehicle inspection.

This is not a general check to be made before every departure: the distributor is part of certain ignition systems and is not present on all bus engines. The vehicle's safety condition is checked instead.
It is false that the requirements on the registration document can be disregarded: transporting a person in a wheelchair must comply with the vehicle's type-approval and operating conditions.
Field S.1 indicates the number of seats, including the driver's seat. Standing places, when provided, are indicated in field S.2.
The number of people specified on the registration document must not be exceeded: the limits for seated and standing places apply.
Standing passengers hold onto the designated handholds to reduce the risk of falling if the vehicle brakes suddenly.
Passengers are not normally required to clean their seat after use; they must, however, avoid dirtying or damaging the vehicle.
While the vehicle is moving, standing passengers must hold onto the designated handholds, including in case of sudden braking.
Standing passengers must also follow safety rules, including holding onto the designated handholds while the vehicle is moving.
Emergency windows should not normally be broken: they are used for evacuation when necessary.
The doors must be used according to the boarding and alighting signs to allow passengers to move in an orderly and safe manner.
If load combinations are specified, the one used and its corresponding limits on places and load must be respected.
When passengers are standing, careful, anticipatory driving limits sudden braking and manoeuvres that could make them fall.
Standing passengers are permitted when the registration document provides for standing places, up to the number indicated.
The hammers are not souvenirs: they must remain available on board to break the windows in an emergency.
There is no general ban: wheelchair users can travel in the designated spaces on suitably equipped buses.
They must not all gather at the back: standing passengers spread out along the aisle or in the designated spaces without obstructing the doors.
Free space in the aisle is not enough: standing places must be provided for in the registration document, and the stated limits must not be exceeded.
Standing passengers spread out along the aisle or in the designated spaces, avoiding crowding and obstruction of movement on board.
It is not always prohibited: wheelchair users can be transported on buses or minibuses equipped with a designated, accessible space.
There is no general ban on bringing a wheelchair on board: on suitably equipped vehicles, the person can enter the designated space with it.
Being close to the front door alone is not enough: the wheelchair must be placed in the designated space equipped for it on the vehicle.
Service needs do not authorise exceeding the passenger limits stated in the registration document.
Transporting a person in a wheelchair requires a suitably equipped bus, with appropriate access and a designated space.
The number of seated people must not exceed the number of seats specified on the registration document; field S.1 also includes the driver.
The wheelchair and its passenger must be positioned in the designated space, using the devices required to secure it safely.
People with reduced mobility can travel on the bus; accessible vehicles have features that make it easier for them to board and be accommodated.
Available space does not allow an unlimited number of people to board: the number of standing places shown in the document must be respected.
Not leaning out of or throwing objects from the windows protects passengers and other road users.
It is false that no precautions are needed: with standing passengers, the driver must drive smoothly and avoid sudden manoeuvres that could make them fall.
Field S.2 indicates any standing places. In the situation described in the quiz, if none are indicated, passengers travel seated in the authorised seats.
Field S.2 indicates the authorised standing places: if any are provided, they may be occupied up to the number indicated.
Passengers may travel standing only if the vehicle has authorised places for that purpose and within the limits indicated.
Avoiding pushing and leaning on seated people reduces the risk of collisions and protects other passengers.
The reference to S.1 is incorrect: this field indicates seats; any standing places are indicated in S.2.
Keeping the doors clear allows passengers to board and get off without obstruction.
The vehicle must remain securely braked while passengers board or get off, to prevent movements that could make them fall.
It is false that emergency exits must be opened: the designated doors are used for normal boarding and getting off, while emergency exits are for use when needed.
Passengers must get off in a safe place: on scheduled services, the designated stops are used, taking care not to expose passengers to traffic.
It is false that a personal need requires the driver to make a phone call: during boarding and alighting, the driver must monitor the process and avoid distractions.
Before moving off again, the driver checks that boarding and alighting are complete and that people are safe.
It is false that hazard lights are always required during boarding and alighting: they are used when the situation calls for a hazard warning, not automatically at every stop.
If provided, a ramp or lift allows a wheelchair user to board and get off safely; it must be used according to the vehicle's procedures.

The quiz considers assistance to facilitate access necessary, for example by using the ramp when provided. The specific duties depend on the service and its conditions, however: they do not always involve personal physical assistance.
The driver must monitor operations at the doors: unrelated activities can divert attention from passenger safety.
The scheduled times at stops help keep the service regular; traffic or other obstacles can nevertheless cause delays.

The quiz considers it false that eating on board at the terminus is permitted: stopping alone does not automatically make eating on the vehicle permissible. However, the applicable rules may depend on the company and the circumstances.
The bus must move off again only after the doors have been closed, to avoid exposing passengers to the risks of travel.
The doors are checked before moving off again: an unclosed door can endanger passengers.
If circumstances beyond anyone's control require a diversion, informing passengers helps them understand how the journey will continue.
Checking the vehicle at the end of the route helps find forgotten belongings and start the process of returning them according to company procedures.
A service communication can be used to report an emergency to the control centre. While the vehicle is moving, the rules on using devices and driving safely still apply.

The quiz generally considers it inappropriate for the driver to eat in the area reserved for passengers, even during a stop: this area should be kept clean and available for service. The statement expresses a rule of conduct in the quiz, not a proven general legal prohibition for every stop.
Hot weather does not justify driving with the doors open: before moving off again, the driver must check that they are closed, for passenger safety.
There is no preference for two-tone horns: the horn must be used sparingly and for road safety purposes.
A ban for the entire period of duty is too broad: the driver may eat during an appropriate break, respecting the rules for the vehicle and the service. Local provisions may be more restrictive.
A ban for the entire period of duty is too broad: smoking is not permitted during the journey or on board, but a break outside the vehicle is different. More restrictive local provisions may apply.
As a rule, the driver does not bring their own animals on board while on duty. The requirement also depends on the applicable regulations.
The driver must not interrupt the service merely as a personal decision: they may do so when there are justified reasons, such as an obvious danger or circumstances beyond their control.
The driver must treat passengers fairly and courteously, remaining respectful even in difficult situations.
A service disruption does not authorise the driver to change the price on their own initiative: the company's agreements and conditions apply.
Being a municipal employee does not automatically entitle someone to free hire: the price of the service is agreed with the customer.
The driver is not required to transport anything at all: luggage and other objects are subject to capacity and safety limits and conditions of carriage.
Driving is entrusted to personnel authorised and qualified for the service; the driver must not hand over control to unauthorised outsiders.
There is no obligation to converse to reassure passengers: while driving, the driver must above all remain attentive and may communicate when necessary without compromising safety.
The driver must not smoke during the journey: the ban protects passengers and the safety of the service.
The ban does not apply to everyone other than passengers: necessary communications are possible, provided they do not distract the driver.
Before opening or closing the doors, the driver must check that the manoeuvre is safe, avoiding hitting or endangering passengers.
The driver must not fulfil every individual request to the detriment of others: they must protect the safety and rights of all passengers.
